synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
On the night of her father’s birthday, in front of two hundred guests, Aurelia Song’s mother raises a glass and announces that her daughter’s jewellery boutique is losing four million a year and will close in January. Aurelia walks out onto the balcony in gold silk, shaking, doing sums in her head. A stranger at the far end gives her his coat.

Three days later, the stranger walks into her boutique and asks to rent it. His name is Chen Si. He runs the Syndicate. He wants her shop for his business. She sets a price instead: a seat at his table.

Then she proposes. Eleven pages, in red ink, with terms. Clause nine is about the bedroom. Clause ten is a single word.

Between them stand a mother who loves only winners, a vice-minister who framed his father, a poisoned glass of wine on New Year’s Eve, a traitor at the table, and a woman who has never once in her life been loved without having to win.

The Woman Who Sets the Price is a sharp, glamorous, power-couple romance about a queen who refuses to be a title, and a man who never once asks her to win.

The main story is told across four volumes. New chapters are added as they are written; the side stories at the end can be read any time. Aurelia and Chen Si first appear in Every Flower in the Shop and Proof by Induction, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This book has some dark moments:

• A parent who humiliates her daughter in public, and emotional coercion within a family

• Organised crime, with threats and violence mostly off the page, and a car attack (A Snake in the Syndicate)

• A poisoning, intensive care and a long recovery (Volume Three)

• A panic attack and its aftermath, and therapy (The Word Is Milan)

• Memories of a parent’s wrongful arrest and death in custody, and of a riot and a stabbing in a juvenile detention centre (The Sewer, Nineteen Years Ago)

• Consensual power-play love scenes between a married couple, with a contract, orders, blindfolds, silk ties and a safe word. They are sensual but not explicit

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Aurelia Song was the rival in Every Flower in the Shop: gold, sunglasses, a slap in the rain, a running score. I wanted to know who she was at two in the morning, when nobody was watching her walk. This is her book.

The crime is kept at the level of a story; nothing here is a how-to. The jewellery is as real as I could make it: piercing saws, gravers, box links soldered one at a time, rouge on the wheel for the last pass.

Thank you for reading. Second is just the first of the ones who kept going.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
AURELIA — Aurelia’s jewellery boutique on Harbour Road.
The Syndicate — The organisation Chen Si runs. Thirty years old, and older than him.
The terms — Aurelia’s price for laundering money through her shop: a share, real pieces, the books, no lies, a seat at the table.
The marriage agreement — Eleven clauses, renewable after ten years, when the Wife may rewrite every one. At the renewal, he adds a twelfth and a thirteenth.
Clause twelve — The Wife is not the Husband’s queen.
The word — The safe word written into the agreement. It is “Milan.”
Numero Uno — The necklace she named at two in the morning, after a phone call with her mother.
The Jade Hall — A restaurant on Temple Street with a round table for twelve. It has belonged to the Syndicate for thirty years.
The house on the Peak — Her parents’ house, where the party for her father’s fifty-seventh birthday was held.
The Song Group — Her father’s company.
The Pearl — The restaurant booked for New Year’s Eve, same as always.
Tesoro — Her father’s name for her, from before Vienna.

chapters.title: The Balcony Where He Lent Her His Coat
chapters.desc: Her mother closes her shop in the middle of a birthday toast. Out on the balcony, a stranger lends her his coat and doesn’t try to make it better.
chapters.epigraph: “Because you’re cold.”
chapters.content:
October had always been Aurelia Song’s favourite month. By half past nine on the night of her father’s fifty-seventh birthday, she thought she might be about to hate it.

The ballroom of the house on the Peak was full. Two hundred guests in black tie and old diamonds, the long windows open to the harbour lights, a string quartet playing something expensive enough that nobody recognised it. Her father was by the fireplace being loud and happy, with a cigar he wasn’t supposed to have. Her mother stood at the foot of the staircase in grey silk, as she always did at her own parties, so that everyone had to look up to her.

Aurelia stood beside her in champagne-gold silk cut on the bias, wearing a necklace from her own autumn collection. Diamonds and pale sapphires, set off-centre on purpose, so that the line of it ran a little to the left of her throat like a hand resting there. She’d spent three weeks choosing the stones. Enzo had spent two more arguing with her about the setting, and lost.

Vittoria Conti Song raised her glass, and the room turned.

“To family,” she said. “To legacy. To knowing when something has served its purpose, and having the courage to move on.”

Aurelia smiled, because she always smiled when her mother spoke in public. Her fingers tightened on the stem of her glass.

“Which brings me to some wonderful news.” Her mother turned towards her, and two hundred faces turned with her. “The little shop on Harbour Road will be closing its doors in January. It has lost four million this year, and four million the year before. We’ve decided it’s time to stop indulging sentimental projects and concentrate on things with a future.”

For one second Aurelia didn’t understand.

Then she understood completely. The little shop. Hers. The label she’d started at eighteen at a kitchen table with a borrowed saw, the shop she’d opened at twenty in the ground floor of a Song Group building, the five years of her life she’d put into the windows on Harbour Road. Her mother had just closed it in a toast, between the canapés and the cake.

Somebody laughed politely. Somebody else said congratulations, as if it were an engagement.

“Mother,” said Aurelia, low.

Vittoria didn’t look at her. “We’ll discuss it later, darling.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“There’s nothing to discuss. The lease is in the Group’s name. The decision’s been made.”

Aurelia looked round the room. Nobody seemed uncomfortable. Her father, by the fireplace, had stopped smiling and was looking at his cigar. Nobody else had noticed that she’d stopped breathing properly.

She put her glass down on a passing tray.

“Excuse me,” she said, and didn’t wait to be excused.

✦ ✦ ✦

The balcony doors shut behind her and took the music with them.

The October air was cold on her bare shoulders. She walked to the stone balustrade and put both hands flat on it, and stood there, and did not cry. She had been taught not to by an expert. She was furious and humiliated, and so disappointed that it had gone somewhere under her ribs and lodged there like a swallowed stone, and her mother was not going to see her cry about something she’d made with her own hands.

So she did sums instead. Four million was a lie. The shop had lost one point six last year, because the Group charged her rent at twice the market rate and called it support, and it would have broken even by spring. Two clients in the room tonight had pieces on order. Enzo had a mortgage. Lily had a sister in her final year at school. Forty-one working days to January. She ran the numbers twice in her head and they came out the same both times, which was the worst part.

Below the Peak the city poured down to the water in streams of white and red. Somewhere down there people were going home, opening a bottle of wine, complaining about their day. She’d have given the necklace for an ordinary evening.

“You’ll catch cold,” said a man’s voice behind her.

She turned.

He was standing by the doors, one gloved hand in the pocket of a black overcoat. Slight, and still. Neat black hair with a soft fringe, fine features, a face that gave nothing away. He wore a white shirt open at the collar under a black suit, and black leather gloves, at a party, indoors, as though he might need to leave at any moment without touching anything. She hadn’t heard him come out.

“I’m fine,” said Aurelia.

His eyes went to her shoulders. “That wasn’t what I asked.”

“You didn’t ask anything.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “Fair.”

He took off the overcoat. Before she could tell him not to, he’d crossed the balcony and put it round her shoulders, and stepped back again at once, as if he’d delivered something and was waiting for a signature. It was heavy and still warm from him. It smelled of cedar, and ink, and faintly of cold coffee.

“You don’t have to,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because you’re cold.”

It was such a plain answer that she had nothing to say to it.

He didn’t ask why she was out here alone. He didn’t tell her the evening was lovely or that she should go back in and enjoy herself, or that her mother surely hadn’t meant it. He came and stood at the balustrade, a little distance from her, and looked at the city, and let the silence be. After a while she realised her hands had stopped shaking on the stone.

“Do you always lend your coat to women you don’t know?” she said eventually.

“No.”

“So I’m special.”

He turned his head and looked at her properly, the first time he’d done it, with dark, calm eyes that seemed to be taking careful notes.

“Would you like to be?”

Aurelia blinked. He hadn’t said it as a line. He’d said it as if it were a perfectly reasonable question with a yes or a no at the end of it, and he was prepared to wait for either. She looked away first, which she never did.

“You’re very sure of yourself.”

“Sometimes.”

“How fortunate for you.”

She drew the coat closer. He said nothing for a minute. Then, in exactly the same tone:

“May I ask you something else?”

“Depends what it is.”

“Would you let me kiss you?”

She turned so fast her hair caught on her mouth. “What?”

He didn’t look embarrassed. He didn’t look anything. “Would you let me kiss you?”

Men at these parties came at her with compliments and business cards and conversations they’d rehearsed in the car. This one had said perhaps forty words to her, lent her his coat, and asked to kiss her as if he were asking the time.

“You don’t know my name.”

“That’s true.”

“You don’t know anything about me.”

“I know you made that necklace.” He looked at it, not at her throat, at the stones. “The setting’s unusual. The stones aren’t symmetrical. It shouldn’t work, and it does, so I assume you meant it.”

She looked at him more carefully. “You know jewellery?”

“Enough to see when it’s good.”

“That’s a dangerous thing to tell me.”

“Why?”

“I might start asking you questions.”

“I wouldn’t mind.”

She almost smiled. Almost. She was deciding, with a certain amount of astonishment, what the answer to his question actually was, when the balcony door opened behind them.

“Mr. Chen?” A man in a dark suit, with a tablet and an apologetic face. “Your car’s ready. And Mr. Song’s been asking for you.”

“Give me a minute, Qian.”

“Of course.” The door closed again.

Aurelia turned back slowly.

There were several Chen families in the city. There was only one whose name she’d heard all evening said in that particular way, a little lower than the rest of the sentence, the way people spoke of weather that had sunk ships. The man who’d bought three luxury retail groups in two years without his name ever appearing in a headline. The man her father had been so pleased to have at his party, and so careful never to be photographed beside.

“You’re Chen Si,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You might have mentioned it.”

“Would it have changed anything?”

She considered him honestly. “Probably.”

“Then I’m glad I didn’t.”

She narrowed her eyes at him, and he smiled, a small one, and it changed his whole face. He looked a great deal less frightening when he smiled, which she suspected made him more dangerous, not less.

“Go inside,” he said. “It’s getting colder.”

“Are you always this used to giving orders?”

“Only sensible ones.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then I’ll stand here until you’re ready.”

She looked at him. Then she laughed, short and surprised, the first real sound she’d made all night.

He watched her do it with an expression she couldn’t read.

“There,” he said.

“What?”

“That suits you better.”

It made her feel more exposed than her mother’s toast had. She pulled the coat tight round her and walked to the doors.

“Goodnight, Mr. Chen.”

“Chen Si.”

“Goodnight, Chen Si.”

“Goodnight, Miss Song,” he said, and she went back into the ballroom without looking round, with his coat still on, and two hundred people watched her cross the floor in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed at the balustrade until the doors had closed.

“Song Weiren’s elder daughter,” said Qian, at his elbow again.

“Yes.”

“The Group’s been negotiating the surrender of the Harbour Road lease since August. There are several supplier agreements tied to the premises.”

Chen Si held out his gloved hand for the tablet, and didn’t take it when it came.

“Her private accounts. Her suppliers. Who she owes and who owes her. The ownership of that building, and every charge on it.”

Qian looked up. “All of it?”

“All of it.”

“May I ask why?”

Chen Si looked through the glass at the gold dress going up the staircase, past her mother, without stopping.

“Because I want to know exactly what they’re taking from her,” he said. “And find out who holds the freehold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home a little after midnight and didn’t turn on the lights.

Her mother’s message arrived while she was still standing in the hall. Don’t make tonight more difficult than it needs to be. We’ll discuss the shop when you’re ready to be reasonable. Aurelia read it, and put the phone face down on the hall table, and went upstairs.

She took the necklace off and laid it on the dressing table. She didn’t take the coat off. She ought to have sent it back with the driver. Instead she sat on the edge of the bed with it round her shoulders, in the dark, which was ridiculous, because she didn’t know the man and what she did know of him was bad. But for the first time that whole evening somebody had seen that she was hurt and hadn’t asked her to explain it, or fix it, or smile.

She fell asleep in it.

At 8:17 the next morning the housekeeper brought an envelope up on a tray. Thick ivory paper. Her name on the front in black ink, in a hand so neat it looked engraved.

Miss Song,

I believe we have an unfinished conversation. You left with my coat. I would prefer to collect it in person.

Regarding Harbour Road, I would like to discuss an arrangement. I don’t make sentimental investments. I do recognise valuable things.

Perhaps we can agree on a price.

Chen Si

She read it twice. At the bottom, in the same ink but smaller, as though added after the rest had been sealed and then unsealed again:

For the record, the other question remains open.

Aurelia Song sat on her bed in a dressing gown and a stranger’s overcoat, and despite herself, smiled.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wanted to Rent Her Shop
chapters.desc: He comes to her shop offering to wash his money through it. She crosses out his terms in red ink and names her own price.
chapters.epigraph: “Your hands are important.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter past eleven on the Tuesday after the party, Chen Si walked into Aurelia’s shop on Harbour Road and asked her to help him commit a crime. He did it very politely.

She was behind the counter with a loupe in her eye, looking into a sapphire that a dealer had sworn was unheated and that she was fairly sure had been cooked. The morning came in through the tall front windows across the velvet trays, and Lily was in the back with the kettle, and the bell over the door rang.

“Good morning,” Aurelia said, without looking up. “We’re open.”

“I can see that.”

She knew the voice at once. Her hand stopped. She took the loupe out of her eye and put it down.

He was standing just inside the door in a grey suit and a white shirt, no gloves this time, hair neat, with the air of a man who had never once been inconvenienced by the world. He was holding a paper cup.

She looked at the cup. Then at him.

“You came.”

“I did.”

“For your coat?”

“Not entirely.”

“What a pity. I’d begun to think you were sentimental.”

“Would that be a problem?”

“An inconvenience.”

The corner of his mouth moved. She found she had remembered exactly what his face did when he smiled, which annoyed her.

“Good morning, Miss Song.”

“Mr. Chen.”

“We’d agreed on Chen Si.”

“We agreed on nothing. You wrote me a letter.”

“And you smiled when you read it.”

She stared at him. He put the cup down on the glass in front of her.

“Your usual.”

An iced oat latte, no syrup, a little more ice than anyone sensible would want in October. Exactly as she ordered it, from the café across the road, every morning at nine.

“How do you know that?”

“I have a good memory.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“Would you prefer a dishonest one?”

“I’d prefer to know how a man who’s met me once knows how I take my coffee.”

He glanced over his shoulder at the café. Behind its window the young barista was watching them with her mouth open. When she saw Aurelia look, she ducked behind the machine.

“The girl who works there is very enthusiastic,” said Chen Si.

“Did you ask her?”

“I bought a coffee.”

“That’s all?”

“I also asked her to stop drawing hearts on your cups.”

Aurelia blinked. “You what?”

“She was drawing them quite often.”

There was a pause, and then Aurelia laughed, because the alternative was to throw the latte at him.

“You told a nineteen-year-old to stop drawing hearts.”

“She was wasting time.”

“On hearts.”

“Apparently.”

“You really are a terrible man.”

“So I’m told,” he said, entirely untroubled, and she picked up the coffee and drank some, and hated that it was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him to the consultation table at the back, under the good light, and sat in the chair furthest from his. He noticed. He didn’t say anything.

“You mentioned an arrangement,” she said. “Let’s hear it.”

“Your shop has a good name, a loyal list of clients, and stock of a value that makes a high turnover believable.” He laid a slim black folder on the table. “Some of my associates have money that needs to become something else. Fine jewellery is small, it holds its value, and nobody questions the price of a beautiful thing. Your business could be the place where one becomes the other.”

Aurelia looked at him, and at the folder, and at him.

“You want to launder money through my shop.”

He didn’t blink. “Yes.”

“You’re unbelievable.”

“I’ve heard that too.”

“Do you practise saying these things in a mirror?”

“Not usually.”

“You should,” said Aurelia, and opened the folder.

It was beautifully made. Projections, a structure of companies with harmless names, a schedule of what would come in and what would go out and how long it would sit in between. Nothing that would have taught a stranger how to do it. Enough to tell her he’d done it many times before. She read every page while he sat perfectly still opposite her, and when she got to the end she closed it.

“No.”

He folded his hands. “Would you like to hear the rest?”

“No.”

“The arrangement would secure your premises for five years.”

“No.”

“Your suppliers would have guaranteed orders.”

“No.” She smiled at him, not nicely. “Do you know what I find interesting about men like you, Mr. Chen? You think everyone has a price.”

“Everyone has a price.”

“How depressing.”

“What’s yours?”

She looked at him for a long, level second. Then she took the front sheet out of the folder, the page with his terms on it, and stood up and went to the counter and came back with the red fountain pen she used to correct Enzo’s invoices.

She sat down and began to cross things out.

He watched her do it. He didn’t interrupt, not once. She struck through his fee, and his five years, and his structure of companies, line by line, and wrote in the margins in a small upright hand that got steadily faster, and pressed hard enough in places to go through. At the bottom she wrote a number and ruled a line under it. Then she turned the page round and pushed it across the table to him with one finger.

“Twenty per cent.”

“Of what?”

“Of everything that moves through my shop. And a partner’s name on the papers, not a commission. If I’m taking the risk, I’m not taking it as your till.”

His eyes went down the page. “Six conditions.”

“Six.”

“Go on.”

“One. The shop stays mine. My designs, my stones, my staff, my windows. You don’t touch any of it.” He inclined his head. “Two. Every piece that’s sold is real. It exists, I made it, it’s worth what the label says because I set the price. No empty boxes. No paper diamonds.”

“Reasonable.”

“Three. Your associates never come near my people. Nobody approaches Lily or Enzo, nobody asks them to hide anything or sign anything, nobody so much as buys them a coffee.” She looked at the cup. “Four. I see the books. Mine, and every one of yours that touches mine.”

“Agreed.”

“Five. You don’t lie to me. The first time you do, it ends, and I don’t negotiate.”

He looked at her for a moment before he answered. “Without negotiation?”

“Without negotiation.”

“Very well.”

“Six.” She put the pen down. “You don’t use my family. You don’t go to my mother, or my father, or my sister, and you don’t make deals behind my back, and you don’t use anything you know about my life to push me.”

Something moved in his face. It was small, and it was gone almost before it was there, but she was watching for it, and she saw it.

“That’s a very specific condition.”

“Your proposal was very specific.”

He read the six conditions again. Then he sat back.

“Twenty per cent. Partner.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve negotiated rather hard.”

“I thought you liked women who knew what they wanted.”

“I do.” He looked up from the paper to her face, and stayed there. “This one especially.”

She looked down at the contract so he wouldn’t see what that did. “Read it properly before you agree.”

“I have.”

“And?”

“All six.”

“Just like that?”

“Just like that.” He held out his hand for the pen. She gave it to him, and instead of signing he turned to the empty space under her sixth condition and wrote, in that engraved hand:

7. Thursday dinner.

Aurelia stared at it.

“What is that?”

“Dinner.”

“I can read.”

“Then I don’t see the difficulty.”

“You can’t put a dinner invitation in a business contract.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s ridiculous.”

“Then cross it out.”

She picked up the pen. He watched her do it. She held it over the line for one second longer than she meant to, and then struck it through.

“Disappointing,” said Chen Si, and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the counter for the partnership papers her lawyer had drawn up for an investor who’d never materialised, and left him at the table. Behind her, his phone buzzed.

Qian: The background report is complete.

He opened it and went down it without much interest. Schools, companies, a flat in her own name, two speeding fines. Then one entry, near the end, from the year she’d turned eighteen.

Final year, overall rank. First: Lin Elowen. Second: Aurelia Song.

There was a photograph from a prize-giving. Aurelia on a stage in a school blazer holding a silver cup, her face composed and her eyes not; beside her a smaller girl with tired eyes and a bigger cup, smiling politely for the camera. Chen Si looked at it for some time. Then he looked across the shop at the woman sorting papers at the counter, with a pencil now pushed into her hair.

He rang Qian.

“Why is the Lin girl in this?”

“She’s the one name that comes up every time anybody at that school talks about Miss Song. Miss Song was ranked first for two years. In the last year, she wasn’t.”

“Was that important?”

“To her mother, apparently very.”

Chen Si closed the file. “Keep it. And nobody contacts anyone from her school.”

A brief pause. “Understood.”

He’d put the phone face down by the time she came back with the papers.

“I’ve got a supplier at one,” she said.

“I won’t keep you.”

“Wonderful.”

She reached for the folder. He didn’t let go of it at once. She looked at his hand, and then at his face.

“Something else?”

“Your hand.”

She looked down. There was a streak of red ink along the side of her first finger and across her knuckle, where she’d been pressing hard.

“Oh.”

“You were writing with feeling.”

“I was making a point.”

“I noticed.”

He reached for her hand, and she went still, and he stopped, at once, an inch away.

“May I?”

She looked at him. Then she put her hand in his.

His fingers were warm and dry. He turned her hand a little towards the light and looked at the ink as he’d looked at the necklace, as if it told him something.

“You could have used black.”

“Red’s more visible.”

“Clearly.” His thumb rested in the middle of her palm.

Then, without looking away from her, he lifted her hand and put his mouth to the inside of her wrist.

He didn’t pull her closer. There was only the warmth of his mouth on the thin skin over her pulse, his hand holding hers up, and a pause, just long enough, before he let her go. Her pulse gave her away completely. He felt it. Of course he did.

“Your hands are important,” he said.

She swallowed. “They’re very good at signing contracts.”

“I meant the other thing they do.” He glanced at the cases, at the gold on the velvet. “You’re very good at it.”

For once she couldn’t think of a single clever thing to say.

He let go of her hand and went back to the papers as though nothing had happened. She looked down at her wrist. The ink was still on her finger. There was nothing at all on her wrist, and she could feel exactly where it had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past twelve he’d signed every page. She went to the back and came out with his black overcoat over her arm, brushed and folded, and held it out.

“Your coat.”

He took it and put it on. “Twenty per cent,” she said, checking the last signature. “Six conditions. And you agreed to all of them without negotiating.”

“I negotiated.”

“When?”

“Just now. I put in Thursday.”

“And I crossed it out.”

“You did.”

“You really don’t give up.”

“No.”

“Is that a personality flaw?”

“Very possibly.”

She laughed under her breath. He went to the door, and she found she’d followed him there.

“Chen Si.”

He turned.

“Don’t think that because I’ve agreed to work with you, you can do whatever you like.”

“I wouldn’t.”

“And don’t have me investigated again.”

He looked straight at her. “I’ll be careful.”

“That isn’t the same as agreeing.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.” He opened the door, and the bell rang, and he stopped on the step. “Thursday. Seven.”

“I haven’t said yes.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you telling me the time?”

“Because I’m going to ask again,” said Chen Si, and went out to the black car at the kerb.

It was only when the car had turned the corner that she realised she’d never asked how he knew where the shop was. Then she remembered that it was his job to know.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past one her phone buzzed.

Unknown: Have you had lunch?

Aurelia: Who is this?

Unknown: Your partner.

She looked across the road. The barista was wiping the counter with great concentration.

Aurelia: How did you get this number?

Unknown: Your loyalty card at the café.

Aurelia: You went through my loyalty card?

Unknown: I asked the girl for your number. She gave it to me.

Aurelia: That’s extremely inappropriate.

Unknown: I agree. I should have asked you.

She stared at that. It was the last thing she’d expected him to say.

Aurelia: Yes. You should have.

Unknown: I’ll ask next time.

Aurelia: There won’t be a next time.

Unknown: Then I’ll make this one count. Thursday. Seven. Dinner.

Aurelia: You’re relentless.

Unknown: You still haven’t said no.

She put the phone face down on the counter. Then she picked it up again and saved the number, and after some thought, called it Mr. Thursday.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-four minutes past one, in the back of the car, Chen Si’s phone buzzed.

Qian: The revised agreement has gone to the lawyers. One question. Are we going ahead with Thursday?

Through the tinted glass the shop was still just in sight at the end of the road. She was behind the counter with a customer, holding a ring up to the window, and smiling the way she had on the balcony when she laughed.

Chen Si: Yes.

Qian: A business dinner?

He looked at the shop until the car turned.

Chen Si: No. This one is mine.

chapters.title: Aurelia Negotiates a Don Into a Corner
chapters.desc: She takes him to a basement with no menu and finds a thief in his books before the fish goes cold. Under a streetlamp, he stops waiting.
chapters.epigraph: “I only drink what I take.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to seven on Thursday his phone lit up on the seat beside him.

He had no idea that she’d saved him as Mr. Thursday. On his screen there was only her name, and under it:

Aurelia: Don’t wear a tie.

He looked down at the dark blue one he’d just knotted.

Chen Si: Is that an instruction?

Aurelia: A warning. You’ll look ridiculous where we’re going. Bring money.

Chen Si: How much?

Aurelia: Enough to pay for dinner. Don’t embarrass me.

He took the tie off and folded it into his pocket. Across the car Qian looked up from his tablet, saw his employer’s face, and looked down again at once.

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was in a lane behind the old furniture market, where most of the shutters were already down for the night. No sign. A faded red lantern over a wooden door and a flight of steps going down, and Aurelia standing at the top of them in a camel coat and flat shoes, with her hair pushed back under a velvet band.

“This is it?” he said.

“Did you expect a chandelier?”

“I expected a sign.”

“How unimaginative,” said Aurelia, and went down.

The basement was hot and loud and smelled of ginger, garlic and soy. Six wooden tables, all full but one. A television in the corner playing a variety show from twenty years ago with the sound off. Behind the counter, an old man in a vest looked up and lit like a lamp.

“Little Aurelia!”

Her whole face changed. “Uncle Fan.”

“Three weeks! Where’ve you been? Getting thinner?” He came round the counter, patted her shoulder twice, and then saw who was standing behind her. His face didn’t change much. It changed enough.

“Who’s this?”

“My business partner.”

Chen Si held out his hand. “Chen Si.”

Old Fan looked at the hand. He didn’t take it. “Chen.”

“Yes.”

“Which Chen?”

“Uncle Fan,” said Aurelia.

“What? I’m asking.”

Chen Si lowered the hand without any sign of offence. “The ordinary kind.”

Old Fan looked at him a moment longer, then snorted and pointed at the empty table by the kitchen door. “Sit. Both of you.”

“See,” Aurelia murmured, “he likes you.”

There was no menu. Old Fan brought what he’d decided they’d eat: steamed fish with ginger and spring onion, braised tofu, greens fried hard with garlic, prawns in their shells, a clay pot of rice with a crust on the bottom. Aurelia picked up her chopsticks before he’d sat down.

“You chose this place,” he said.

“When I want something good, I come here.”

“Not when you want to impress someone.”

“Do you need impressing?”

“No.”

“Then we’re both lucky,” she said, and started on the fish, and almost at once met a bone she didn’t like. He watched her fight it for a little while. Then he put his chopsticks down.

“Give it to me.”

“I can manage.”

“I know. You’re taking too long.”

She gave him a look and put the piece in his bowl. He took the flesh off the bone in long, unhurried movements, lifted out the fine bones one at a time with the tips of his chopsticks and laid them on the edge of the plate in a neat row, and put the clean fish back in front of her. He went on eating his own dinner as if he’d done nothing at all.

She looked at the fish. “Most men would tell me to be careful.”

“Would you listen?”

“No.”

“Then this is more efficient.”

She laughed, and ate it, and he watched her do it, and decided that he liked how she ate here. At her father’s party she’d barely touched a plate. She’d spent the night smiling at people she plainly disliked and pretending her mother hadn’t just closed her life in a toast. Here she argued with Old Fan about the ginger, stole two prawns off Chen Si’s side of the table without asking, and laughed without first checking who was looking. He wondered how many people had ever been allowed to see her like this, and found he wanted the number to stay small.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d taken his folder off him before the rice arrived. By the time the fish was a skeleton she’d stopped eating altogether. She had his partnership accounts open on one side of her plate and, beneath them, three sheets from the back of the folder that he hadn’t meant to give her: the ledgers of a furniture importer the Syndicate had owned for nine years.

Forty-one minutes after they’d sat down, she laid three pages side by side on the table and looked up.

“Who runs the furniture accounts?”

He put down his tea. “Why?”

“Because somebody’s stealing from you.”

Nothing moved in him. That was what she’d remember afterwards. Not anger, nothing like anger, only a stillness that seemed to drop the temperature round the table a degree or two.

“How much?”

“About half a million. Since spring.” She turned one sheet round and touched it with the tip of her pen. “Here. And here. Payments to suppliers that don’t match what the suppliers are owed. The difference has been dressed up as freight and storage, which nobody ever checks, because freight is boring. It’s the same three or four lines every month, the same pattern, just under the size anyone would notice.”

“How long have you been looking at these?”

“Forty-one minutes.”

He glanced at his watch.

“Would you like me to take longer?” said Aurelia. “Don’t interrupt.” She tapped the third page. “The amount isn’t the interesting part. It’s how tidy it is. Whoever did this knows your books well enough not to get caught in the ordinary way. They’ve only been careless because they think nobody looks at furniture.” She closed the folder. “Your problem isn’t half a million. Your problem is that someone inside your house thinks you’re too busy to notice.”

“You’re sure.”

“I’m sure there’s money missing. I’m not naming anybody without an independent audit. A proper one. Before anyone does anything.”

He looked at her. “Before anyone does anything,” he repeated.

“I know who you are, Chen Si.” She held his eyes. “Before.”

“Agreed,” he said, after a moment.

“You’re taking it very calmly.”

“Would you prefer I turned the table over?”

She glanced at the prawns. “Absolutely not. Uncle Fan would kill you.”

“Then I’ll restrain myself,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came up into the lane after eight. It had rained while they were underground and the stones were wet and smelled of it. Most of the market had gone dark. He walked beside her with his hands in his coat pockets.

“Half a million,” he said. “In forty-one minutes.”

“Shall I invoice you?”

“Perhaps I should pay you a fee.”

“Perhaps you should stop employing thieves.”

He laughed, low, and she looked sideways at him.

“What?”

“You’re interesting.”

“That’s unfortunate for you.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m starting to think your judgement’s poor.”

“I’ve made worse investments.”

“Speaking of which,” said Aurelia, and stopped under a streetlamp and took a folded sheet out of her bag. “I’ve revised my terms.”

“Already?”

“I did it during dinner.”

“While I was eating.”

“You were perfectly capable of feeding yourself.” She handed it to him.

The first line was in red. Partner’s share: 25%.

“Twenty-five. On Tuesday it was twenty.”

“On Tuesday I hadn’t seen the state of your books.”

“You’re raising your price because you found a problem?”

“I’m raising my price because I found a problem you didn’t know you had.”

He read on. A stronger audit clause. Her approval over any sale through the shop that involved a buyer she hadn’t met. And a separate clause, in a smaller, harder hand, about Milan.

“The Milan route,” said Chen Si.

“My Milan launch, and everything that goes through it. My suppliers there, my workshop, my distribution. It’s handled separately, it’s audited separately, and none of your associates’ money ever goes near it.” Her chin went up a fraction. “My name is going to mean something in Milan. It isn’t going to be your drawer.”

“And if I refuse?”

“Then we don’t have a partnership.”

She said it flatly, without softening it, and didn’t add anything. He folded the paper.

“You’ve become expensive, Miss Song.”

“Then you should ask yourself whether you can afford me.”

He looked at her for a long moment under the lamp. “Agreed.”

“Just like that?”

“Find me another thief,” he said, “and you can have another five.”

“Don’t tempt me.”

He came a step closer, enough that his voice dropped.

“I’m not tempting you. I’m encouraging you.”

There was a convenience store open on the corner. She went in without explaining and came out with two bottles of beer and gave him one, and opened her own on the edge of the step and drank, and sighed.

“Better.”

He looked at the bottle in his hand.

“Are you going to drink that or look at it?” she said.

“I haven’t decided.”

She took it out of his hand, opened it on the step, drank from it, and gave it back to him.

“That was mine,” said Chen Si.

“You weren’t drinking it.”

“I was considering it.”

“Consider faster.”

He looked at the mouth of the bottle, where hers had been. Then he drank from it.

She noticed a second too late. “You drank from that after I did.”

“Yes.”

“Some people mind.”

“I only drink what I take,” said Chen Si.

She choked on her beer and had to turn round and cough into the back of her hand, and when she turned back he was looking entirely innocent.

“Careful,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re very dangerous when you’re being well-mannered.”

“Then you should stop giving me chances,” he said.

They’d come out on the main road, beside a shop that sold paper offerings for the dead, gold paper folded into ingots behind a half-closed shutter. The streetlamp was very bright on the wet pavement. A strand of her hair had come loose from the band and she tucked it back behind her ear, and he watched her do it.

“Aurelia.”

She looked up.

“May I kiss you?”

It came out quietly, and without any of the ease he wore everywhere else. For the first time that evening he seemed to be waiting for something he couldn’t buy or move or negotiate.

“Is this another proposal?”

“No.”

“Conditions?”

“One.” He didn’t look away from her. “You have to want it.”

She put her bottle down on the low ledge of the shop window. Then she came close, reached up and straightened the collar of his coat, which didn’t need straightening, slowly, with both hands, and left them there.

“Yes,” said Aurelia.

He didn’t move at once. He looked at her face as though checking every figure in it. When she didn’t step back, his hand came to her waist, and he bent his head and kissed her.

He’d been patient all evening, through the fish and the ledgers and the red ink, and it was in the kiss, all of it, held back and then not. His other hand came up to her jaw. Her fingers closed in the front of his coat. She’d expected him to be good at it. She hadn’t expected him to make her forget, for several seconds together, that she was supposed to be the one in control, and when he lifted his head she kept her eyes shut.

He rested his forehead against hers.

“Still think I’m a poor investment?”

She opened her eyes. “The early returns are inconclusive.”

“How much more research do you need?”

“Don’t get arrogant.”

“Too late,” said Chen Si, and kissed the corner of her mouth, once, and stepped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

A second black car was waiting at the end of the road, and a man was leaning on it, smoking.

He was young, Chen Si’s age or near it, in a beige suit with the collar open and no tie, black hair swept up and back with one strand that wouldn’t stay. Narrow, heavy-lidded eyes. Heavy rings on two fingers, a silver watch, and a lazy half-smile that didn’t go anywhere near his eyes. He straightened when he saw them, and looked at Aurelia the way a man looks at a lock.

“Si,” he said.

“Brother,” said Chen Si. “This is Aurelia Song.”

“Song Weiren’s girl.”

“Song Weiren’s daughter,” said Aurelia. “Good evening.”

“Zhao Zhendong.” He nodded at her once. “You’re the one who found the furniture money.”

She glanced at Chen Si. He hadn’t told her he’d tell anyone. He must have done it from the table, under it, while she was reading.

“I found that money’s missing,” she said. “I haven’t found who. That needs an audit.”

“Hm,” said Zhao, and dropped his cigarette and put his shoe on it. That seemed to be all he had to say to her. He opened the car door. “You’re late.”

“I’ll call you,” Chen Si told her.

“Not with my café card.”

“No,” he said, and she could hear him smiling. She walked off towards her own car two streets away, and didn’t look back, and knew exactly how long they both watched her go.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She’s sharp,” said Zhao in the car.

Chen Si didn’t answer.

“Doesn’t flatter you.”

“No.”

“Good.” Zhao lit another cigarette and opened the window an inch. “Twenty-five per cent.”

“You heard.”

“You texted me under the table like a schoolboy. Twenty-five, and Milan.” He blew smoke at the gap. “She negotiated you out of more than you meant to give.”

“She did.”

“You look pleased about it.”

“I am.”

Zhao looked at him for a while in the passing light. “Want me to deal with the furniture?”

“When she’s finished,” said Chen Si. “Not before. She asked for an audit.”

“Since when do we do audits?”

“Since Tuesday.”

Zhao made a sound that might have been a laugh. Then, in a different voice: “Don’t make a mess of it, Si.”

“Of what?”

His brother only looked at him, and turned back to the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 11:38 her phone buzzed on the pillow.

Mr. Thursday: Are you home?

Aurelia: Yes.

Mr. Thursday: Your fish was cold by the time you’d finished with my accounts.

Aurelia: Your accounts were more interesting.

Mr. Thursday: That’s a pity. I’d hoped to be the most interesting thing you looked at tonight.

She laughed into the pillow, typed something, deleted it, typed something else.

Aurelia: You’re already too pleased with yourself.

Mr. Thursday: You kissed me.

Aurelia: You asked.

Mr. Thursday: And you said yes. Next time I’ll take you somewhere with a sign.

Aurelia: There won’t be a next time if you insult Uncle Fan.

Mr. Thursday: Then I’ll bone your fish and say nothing.

She looked at that for some time.

Aurelia: You’d better.

✦ ✦ ✦

In his office at the top of the Chen Holdings building, with the city laid out black and gold under the glass, Chen Si opened the file Qian had left on his desk. The furniture accounts. Four months of freight that had never been freighted. And at the end of the trail, past two companies with harmless names, the account where the money had come to rest.

The name on it meant nothing. A company eleven weeks old, registered by a lawyer who registered a great many companies. But she had asked who ran the furniture before he’d told her where to look. She’d gone straight to the freight lines as if she’d seen that trick before, in some other set of books, and she’d said before anyone does anything as if she were afraid of who might be standing in front of him when they did. He thought about her sixth condition. You don’t use my family.

He picked up the phone.

“Don’t approach the account holder,” he said. “Don’t freeze anything. Nobody is to know we’ve seen it.”

“Understood,” said Qian. “Anything else?”

“Find out who at the Song Group signs off on furniture.”

He put the phone down, and looked at her name at the top of his messages for longer than he’d looked at the thief’s.

chapters.title: Aurelia Song Does Not Do Second Place
chapters.desc: He takes away the chairs to see what she will do, so she sits in his. Then she kisses him in it and wins every hand of mahjong in the building.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to win anything for me.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past nine the next Thursday, Aurelia discovered that Chen Si had an unusual idea of hospitality. He’d invited her to a meeting on the thirty-first floor of the Chen Holdings building. He had also, it seemed, had every chair taken out of the room.

“Where are the chairs?” she asked.

The young man at the door looked as if he’d have liked to be somewhere else. “Mr. Chen asked for the room to be prepared differently, Miss Song.”

The long table was immaculate. Water bottles at equal intervals, a screen at the far end with the agenda on it, and a dozen men in dark suits standing about in twos and threes, talking low. Not a chair anywhere. Except at the head of the table, where there was one: tall, black leather, high-backed, obviously his.

“Did he say why?”

“No, Miss Song.”

“What a pity,” said Aurelia, and walked in.

The talking died away as she crossed the room. She put her bag on the table and took out her phone.

Aurelia: Your meeting room has a problem.

Mr. Thursday: What problem?

Aurelia: Someone’s stolen the chairs.

Mr. Thursday: How unfortunate. I’ll have it looked into.

She put the phone away. Then she went to the head of the table and pulled out the black chair.

Somebody cleared his throat. “Miss Song, that seat is—“

“Taken?”

“It’s Mr. Chen’s.”

“Wonderful,” said Aurelia, and sat down in it, and crossed her legs, and set her phone beside the water. “Good morning, gentlemen. Shall we begin?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Next door, Chen Si was watching on a monitor with a cup of coffee in his hand.

“She took my chair,” he said.

“Yes, Mr. Chen,” said Qian.

“Without asking.”

“Yes.”

He drank some coffee. A small smile came and went. Qian, who had worked for him for six years and knew that the smile was not necessarily good news for anyone, said nothing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Before we start,” said Aurelia, “I’d like to be clear what we’re here for. The trade routes, what they cost, and the furniture accounts.”

“That’s right,” said a heavy man on her right, folding his hands.

“Then let’s stay on those.” She turned a page of the report someone had put at her place. “Who wrote this?”

“I did. Kuang Ming.”

“Mr. Kuang, you say the furniture business’s costs went up twelve per cent last quarter.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Market conditions. Freight. Supplier adjustments. Some unexpected expenses.”

“Which suppliers?”

He paused. “Several.”

“Which ones?”

Another pause. She looked up at him, quite pleasantly.

“I’m asking because your report doesn’t name them.”

“We can provide a supplementary document.”

“Please do.” She made a note. “You also call the missing payments delayed settlements.”

“That’s accounts’ preliminary view.”

“Then it should say preliminary. Otherwise someone might mistake it for a fact.”

Nobody spoke. She went on. For twenty minutes she asked questions, and none of them was unkind, and she never raised her voice or interrupted anyone or accused a single person of anything. She asked for figures. She asked for the paper behind the figures. She asked for names. Every vague answer got a more exact question, and every attempt to steer her somewhere else got her back, gently, to where she’d been.

At last a man at the far end of the table leaned back.

“With respect, Miss Song, these matters are usually handled internally.”

“Then you should have handled them internally before half a million went missing.”

The room went very quiet.

“That’s a serious accusation.”

“It’s a discrepancy. I haven’t accused anyone of anything. I’m only sure the numbers don’t match.” She closed the report. “If you’d like to show me they do, I’d be delighted to see the documents.”

He didn’t answer. She smiled at him. “Please. Go on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past ten Qian brought a tablet into the side office.

“Miss Song has asked for the original supplier contracts, the furniture business’s payment history, and the last three quarterly reports. She’d like the audit done by an outside firm. And she’s asked for access to the Milan distribution records.”

“Give her all of it,” said Chen Si, without looking away from the screen.

“She’s still in your chair.”

On the monitor she was leaning forward with one hand flat on his table, explaining something to the heavy man on her right, who was writing it down.

“Leave it,” said Chen Si.

The meeting ran two hours. By the end she’d found three more inconsistencies in the operating reports, put five supplier relationships under review, and set up a separate reporting schedule for everything that touched Milan. She’d also made a room full of men who took instructions from almost nobody listen to her without interrupting once. When they stood up to go she stayed where she was.

“Thank you, gentlemen.”

The last one out stopped at the door. “Mr. Chen will be pleased to hear it went well.”

“Do tell him,” said Aurelia, “that I hope he enjoyed his morning.”

The man looked confused, and left.

She was standing at the window, looking down at the harbour, when the door opened behind her.

“Your men are very hard to impress,” she said, without turning round.

“Are they?”

“They seem to think a question is a personal attack.”

“They’re not used to being asked any.” He came across the room and stopped beside the table, beside the chair. She saw him look at it.

“Something wrong?”

“I was wondering whether you meant to give it back.”

“Eventually.” She went and sat in it again, to make the point, and looked up at him. “Why did you take the chairs away?”

He took a moment over it. “I wanted to see what you’d do.”

“Seriously?”

“Yes.”

“You made me stand, on purpose, in front of twelve of your men.”

“I wanted to see whether you’d ask for a chair.”

“And?”

“You didn’t. You took the one that mattered.”

“If you ever do that again,” said Aurelia, “I’ll have this whole room furnished from a primary school. Little plastic chairs. You can chair your board meetings with your knees round your ears.”

He laughed. It came out of him low and unplanned, and he looked almost surprised by it himself.

“Are you finished with my seat?” he said.

“Not quite.” She turned in the chair to face him. “Come here.”

“Is that an instruction?”

“Would you like it in writing?”

He came. She reached up, took hold of his tie, wrapped the silk once round her fingers and drew him down to her, and kissed him.

She’d decided to, so she did. She took her time over it. His hand came down on the arm of the chair beside her; the other found her waist. He kissed her back slowly at first, and then not slowly, and she felt the exact moment the meeting and the accounts and the men waiting in the corridor went out of him altogether. When she let go of the tie he stayed where he was, bent over her, a hand on each arm of his own chair.

“Was that part of the negotiation?”

“No.”

“Then what was it?”

“Compensation. For two hours of your men’s nonsense.”

“Shall I arrange another meeting?”

She tugged the tie once, and then slid the knot loose and drew it out from under his collar and put it in her bag.

“Don’t push your luck,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seventeen minutes past three the outside auditors confirmed whose account the missing money had gone to.

It belonged to a man called Ye Liang, a junior accountant in the furniture business, thirty-one, who’d been with the company four years and lived with his mother. By four, Sun Wei had come up to the top floor himself to apologise for him.

Sun Wei ran furniture. He’d run it for eleven years, since long before Chen Si had taken it over: a soft-spoken man of fifty with reading glasses on a cord, who sat at Chen Si’s table every Sunday and remembered the birthdays of other people’s children. He stood in front of the desk with his hands folded and said he was ashamed. That he should have seen it. That the boy had been under his roof and he’d trusted him, and he would bring him up here himself, today, if Chen Si wanted.

“Not yet,” said Chen Si. “Leave him his access. I’d like to see what he does with it.”

“Of course.” Sun Wei took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. “I’ve sent Miss Song an orchid. To say sorry, for the trouble. I hope that wasn’t presumptuous.”

“Not at all,” said Chen Si.

When he’d gone, Chen Si sat with the auditors’ report for some time. Ye Liang’s account had received the money. It hadn’t kept it. It had passed most of it on within a week, every time, to another company with a harmless name, and nobody yet knew whose that one was.

At twenty to six he wrote to her.

Chen Si: The account is a clerk’s. Ye Liang. Four years in furniture.

She was in the shop with the Milan papers spread across the counter, and a white orchid in a pot by the till with a card that said With apologies, Sun Wei.

Aurelia: A clerk didn’t think of that.

Chen Si: No.

Aurelia: Someone taught him where to hide it.

Chen Si: Do you know who?

She looked at the message, and didn’t move for some time. There were things she could tell him. Some of them she wanted to. But there was a difference between trusting a man and handing him every weapon she had, and the person on the other end of this was someone she’d known a great deal longer than she’d known Chen Si.

Aurelia: Not yet.

Mr. Thursday: I see.

Aurelia: Do you?

Mr. Thursday: I think so. I’ll wait.

She’d expected him to push. To remind her that it was his money and his house and he had every right. Instead he’d said he would wait. She put the phone down on the counter, face down, and thought that was a great deal more dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past eight he was in the room above the Jade Hall on Temple Street, where the senior men of the Syndicate had been playing mahjong on Thursday nights for thirty years, watching four of them lose money to each other.

Aurelia: Where are you?

Chen Si: Watching mahjong.

Aurelia: How dull. I play better than you.

Chen Si: That’s a confident statement.

Aurelia: Shall I come and prove it?

He sent her the address.

She arrived twenty minutes later in a black silk blouse and narrow trousers, with small diamonds in her ears and her hair down, and every man in the room stood up, and one of them was Sun Wei, who bowed his head to her and said he hoped she liked the orchid.

“It’s beautiful,” she said. “Thank you.”

Chen Si pulled out the empty chair beside his own. “You’re late.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Do you really play, Miss Song?” said Kuang Ming, from the far side of the table, with the air of a man expecting to get his morning back.

“A little,” said Aurelia.

The first game took forty minutes and she won it. The second took thirty-five and she won that too. By the third the men had stopped laughing. She played with an odd mixture of patience and instinct. She never hurried, and she didn’t try to frighten anyone; she simply paid attention, to the tiles and the discards and the faces, and to the small habits a man falls into when he’s hiding something good. She was very quick to see when somebody had become too pleased with his hand.

Between the third game and the fourth Chen Si reached for her hand.

“What?”

“Your rings. They’ll catch.”

She had three on: a diamond band, a pale sapphire, a thin gold signet. She looked at him, and then took them off one by one and put them in his palm, and he laid them out on a square of black velvet beside his teacup in a neat row, the way he’d laid out the bones of her fish.

“You’re good at that.”

“At what?”

“Looking after expensive things.”

“Only expensive things?”

“Don’t get ambitious,” said Aurelia.

He picked up the diamond band and turned it to the lamp. “Who made this?”

“I did.”

“The stones are very well matched.”

“Of course they are.”

He put it back on the velvet. Then, without seeming to think about it, he took her bare hand again and ran his thumb once across the place where the rings had been.

“You’re distracting me,” she said.

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll behave,” said Chen Si, and let go, and she won the fourth game too.

“Where did you learn to play like that, Miss Song?” said one of the men, rueful, pushing his counters across.

“My grandfather. In Milan. Every Sunday, from when I was six.”

“Then you have his gift.”

“No,” said Aurelia, laying out her tiles. “I practised.”

Chen Si looked at her. He liked that more than the winning. It told him something. She hated being second, but she’d never expected the world to hand her first. She worked for it. She studied. And when she lost, she remembered exactly why.

At five to midnight she put down her last tile. “Mahjong.” The table groaned. He gave her back her rings in the order she’d taken them off, the band, the sapphire, the signet, and slid the last one onto her finger himself.

“Do I get a reward,” he said, “for three hours of looking after your jewellery?”

“Would you like a certificate?”

“Something more personal.”

She glanced round the table. Then, under it, where nobody could see, she slid her hand into his. He turned his palm up and held it, and went on looking at the tiles as if nothing had happened at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The corridor outside was quiet. She pressed the button for the lift and watched the numbers over the doors.

“Do you know what my mother used to say about me?” she said. “That I was too competitive.”

“Was she wrong?”

“Probably not.” The numbers climbed. “When I was small I thought that if I came first, everyone would be happy with me. My teachers. My parents. Anyone who was supposed to be proud. Then I grew up and found out that some people will be disappointed in you whatever you do. So I stopped trying to please them.”

“Who are you trying to please now?”

“Myself, perhaps.”

“Good,” said Chen Si.

“That’s all you’ve got?”

“What else would you like?”

“I don’t know. Something encouraging.”

The doors opened. Neither of them moved.

“You don’t have to win anything for me,” he said.

She didn’t answer. It was such a plain thing to say, and it went straight under her ribs to the place where her mother’s toast was still lodged, and sat down beside it. She stepped into the lift. He followed her. When the doors had closed she took his face in both hands and kissed him against the mirrored wall, and he held her by the waist and let her, all the way down to the ground.

“What?” she said, when she let him go. He was smiling.

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’ve been winning,” said Chen Si.

“At what?”

He tucked a strand of her hair behind her ear. “I get to look at you.”

She looked away. It was unfair. She could take a boardroom apart before lunch and win four games of mahjong off the men who ran the city’s underside, and one quiet sentence from him in that low voice made her face burn. She decided she disliked him a little.

His phone buzzed as they came out into the street. He read it, and she saw his face change, only slightly, and close.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing urgent.”

“That’s a terrible lie.”

“You’re very observant.”

“Unfortunately,” said Aurelia.

He thought about telling her. Then he remembered not yet, and put the phone in his pocket, and took her home.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past one he opened Qian’s message again in his office.

Qian had followed the money one company further. The company Ye Liang passed it to had two directors. One of them also sat, with a small share, on the board of a property firm that was eighty per cent owned by the Song Group.

He read it twice. Someone in her family was in this. Perhaps not directly. Perhaps not knowingly. He thought of her sixth condition, and the way she’d written it, pressing so hard the nib had gone through.

His phone buzzed.

Aurelia: I forgot to tell you something. I still have your tie.

Chen Si: I know.

Aurelia: How?

Chen Si: I came home without it.

Aurelia: Goodnight.

Chen Si: Goodnight, sweetheart.

He’d sent it before he could think better of it. Nearly a minute went by.

Aurelia: Who said you could call me that?

Chen Si: May I?

Aurelia: You may apply.

Aurelia: Application pending.

He sat back in his chair, with the Song Group’s name in the file on the desk in front of him, and laughed out loud in the empty office.

chapters.title: The First Ledger She Ever Read
chapters.desc: Her first crate gets through customs at dawn, and she loves every minute. That night at her counter he looks at her mouth, and leaves.
chapters.epigraph: “It can’t hurt.”
chapters.content:
At fourteen minutes to six on a Wednesday morning in the middle of November, Aurelia fell in love with a shipment of furniture.

Not because the furniture was beautiful. It wasn’t, especially: dark walnut tables with dull brass fittings from a workshop in Cantù, north of Milan, bound for a hotel lobby nobody would remember. She was in love with the clearance stamp on the manifest in her hand. CLEARED. And with what was packed inside the third, fourth and fifth crates, between the table legs, in fitted cases lined with grey felt: the first eleven pieces of her Milan collection, made in her own workshop by her own people, which had been travelling for nineteen days on what she’d started calling, in her head, her route.

She read the stamp twice. Then she smiled so broadly that the logistics manager standing beside her on the Iron Docks took half a step back.

“Miss Song?”

She watched the first crate swing up off the deck in the grey light, over the black water, onto the quay. Her necklaces. Her sketches made real. Months of arguments with stone dealers and casters and a man in Valenza who refused on principle to answer the telephone, and an unreasonable number of emails at three in the morning. And now they were here.

“Everything’s cleared, Miss Song.”

“I can see that,” said Aurelia, and laughed out loud on the dock, because she was happy, and for once she didn’t feel any need to hide it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si’s car came through the dock gates at twelve minutes past six. He’d been awake for hours. He’d also had three messages from her before five, none of them a complete sentence.

Aurelia: IT’S HERE

Aurelia: CHEN SI

Aurelia: IT CLEARED

He’d written back Congratulations. That had apparently been insufficient, because there followed a photograph of the manifest, a photograph of the crates, and a photograph of Aurelia standing in front of the crates with her chin up and an expression that could only be called victorious. He’d put on his coat.

He saw her before he was out of the car. She was by the inspection bay in a cream coat and ankle boots with a clipboard held against her chest, talking to a supervisor, her hair tied back anyhow. There was a smudge of dust on her cheek. She was smiling, not politely, not at anyone, just smiling, the way a child smiles when it’s been given the thing it asked for.

He stood beside the car for a moment and watched her.

“Mr. Chen?” said Qian.

“Wait.”

Then she turned, and saw him, and her whole face lit.

“Chen Si!”

She came across the concrete at a pace that was almost a run, and he barely had time to take his hands out of his pockets before she’d reached him.

“You came!”

“I thought I ought to inspect the shipment.”

“Don’t be ridiculous. You came because I told you it cleared.”

“Did you?”

“Three times,” said Aurelia, and took hold of his lapels and pulled him down and kissed him, quick and hard and delighted, on the dock, in front of Qian and the supervisor and two crane drivers. She let go and stood back.

“For luck.”

“It’s already cleared.”

“There’s still plenty that can go wrong.”

“And kissing me prevents it?”

“It can’t hurt.”

“Then you should do it again,” he said.

“Don’t be greedy,” said Aurelia, and gave his lapels one last tug, and went straight back to her crates.

He watched her work. Happiness hadn’t made her careless. If anything she was sharper than usual, checking seals against numbers, making the supervisor open the third case so she could see the felt hadn’t shifted, asking about humidity in the bonded store. She wanted it perfect. He knew that feeling well. He’d just never seen it worn so openly on anyone’s face.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past seven Qian put a phone in his hand.

Three photographs. Aurelia by the crates. Aurelia talking to the manager. Aurelia beside Chen Si, with her hand still on his coat.

“The forklift driver,” said Qian. “From behind the second stack. He says they’re for himself.”

“Says.”

“We haven’t established otherwise.”

Chen Si looked at the last picture for a while. It wasn’t compromising. That wasn’t the point. Somebody had decided they could point a camera at her without her knowing, at his dock, at six in the morning, and he didn’t intend to let that become a habit.

“Delete them.”

“Done.”

“Find out who he sends things to. Then make sure he never works anywhere we own again. Or anywhere anybody we know owns.”

“Understood.”

Across the bay, Aurelia was laughing at something the supervisor had said. She didn’t see the forklift driver walked to the gate between two men, and Chen Si didn’t tell her.

“Breakfast?” he said, when she’d signed the last sheet.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Breakfast.”

“You’re impossible. Something sweet. And coffee. Not from the café opposite my shop.”

“I’ll find somewhere else,” said Chen Si, and she put her arm through his and then looked back once more at the crates going into the store.

“Look at them.”

“They’re beautiful.”

“You’re not just saying that?”

“No.”

She searched his face, and smiled. “I knew you had taste.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By eleven she was back on Harbour Road with her shoes off under the counter. By half past, Mrs. Shao had arrived.

Mrs. Shao was the wife of a banker, fifty or so, in a cream suit and a rope of pearls so well matched that Aurelia could have told her the dealer who’d strung them. She took the chair at the consultation table and accepted tea and said, “Your mother tells me you’re doing rather well.”

“My mother is generous with her opinions.”

Mrs. Shao laughed. “She’s very proud of you.”

Aurelia didn’t answer that. She opened a velvet box. In it lay two emeralds, deep cool green, old-mine stones with their gardens of inclusions plain under the loupe and colour like the inside of a wave.

Mrs. Shao said, “Oh.”

“A matched pair. I’ve kept them together. I think they want to be earrings.”

“How much?”

Aurelia told her. Mrs. Shao’s eyebrows went up.

“You don’t seem keen to negotiate.”

“I’m happy to, if there’s a reason.”

“And what reason might there be?”

“Your husband,” said Aurelia pleasantly. “His secretary rang me last Thursday. She asked if I’d hold these for a private purchase before your anniversary, and whether I could have them set by the twenty-ninth. He wants to surprise you.”

Mrs. Shao looked at the emeralds. Then she laughed out loud. “That man.”

“He has very good intentions.”

“His secretary is more organised than he is.”

“I expect so.”

“I’ll take them myself,” said Mrs. Shao, “and let him think he bought them. Don’t tell him I know.”

“Of course not.”

Mrs. Shao stood, and pulled on her gloves, and looked at her. “Most people who sell me jewellery tell me how beautiful the stones are.”

“And?”

“You told me why my husband wanted them.”

“Beautiful stones are easy to find,” said Aurelia. “Reasons are harder.”

“I like you,” said Mrs. Shao. At the door she turned back. “Don’t let anyone tell you you have to become someone else to be good at this.”

Aurelia stood at the counter for a little while after the bell had stopped.

Aurelia: Sold the emeralds.

Mr. Thursday: Congratulations.

Aurelia: To a banker’s wife. Her husband’s apparently a romantic.

Mr. Thursday: Is that a requirement?

Aurelia: For buying emeralds?

Mr. Thursday: For being a good husband.

Aurelia: I wouldn’t know.

There was a pause long enough for her to put the phone down and pick it up again.

Mr. Thursday: I’ll bear it in mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past seven that evening Qian met her in the lobby of Chen Holdings and took her up to a room on the twenty-third floor with dark shelves, one long table, a glass wall full of the city, and eleven archive boxes along the side. The furniture importer’s books. All of them, back to before Chen Si’s time, the originals, not the copies the auditors had.

He was at the window when she came in. “You’re late.”

“I’m four minutes early.”

“I’ve been waiting.”

“That’s a personal problem,” said Aurelia, and saw the paper bag on the table. Pastries, from the good bakery on Lime Street.

“Dinner,” he said.

“This isn’t dinner.”

“I’ve ordered dinner as well. From somewhere that doesn’t draw hearts.”

“You’re still bothered about that.”

“Not at all.”

“Liar,” she said, and opened the first box.

They worked well together, better than either had expected. She had an eye for the thing that looked ordinary alone and wrong beside its neighbour. She asked when she didn’t know, and listened when he explained, and said so plainly when she disagreed. He’d stopped pretending to supervise within the first hour and was reading the same pages she was, making notes whenever she put her finger on something.

At eight minutes to eleven she found the old ledger.

It was at the bottom of the ninth box, bound in cloth gone soft at the corners, the handwriting in it older and neater than anything in the newer books. She turned the pages slowly. Then she stopped, and ran her finger down a column, and stopped again.

“Chen Si. Come here.”

He came and stood behind her chair.

“This supplier.” She tapped a name. “The freight lines. Same structure, same trick, same three lines a month just under anyone’s notice. Only it’s eleven years ago.” She turned another page, and another. “It’s all through this. It isn’t new. Your clerk didn’t invent anything. He was taught it, or he inherited it. Somebody’s been using this house as a pipe since before you owned it.”

He looked at the dates for a long time. “Nine years,” he said. “I’ve had it nine years.”

“Did you know?”

“No.”

He wasn’t angry, or not where it showed. But something in his face had gone colder, and his hand on the back of her chair had gone still in a way she was learning to watch for. She reached out and closed the ledger.

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Start deciding things before we understand what we’re looking at.”

For a moment she thought he’d argue. Then he took his hand off the chair.

“All right,” said Chen Si. “You’re very comfortable telling me what to do.”

“Someone has to be.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past midnight the pastries were gone and the dinner was cold in its boxes. She’d taken her coat off and was sitting with one foot tucked under her, reading. He’d lost his jacket and his collar was open. She yawned.

“You’re tired,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You just yawned.”

“That proves nothing.”

“You’ll start making mistakes.”

“I don’t make mistakes.”

“Never?”

“Rarely.”

She threw a paper clip at him. He caught it, and set it down beside her notes, perfectly straight.

Somewhere after one they stopped talking about ledgers. She asked him about his first deal, and he said he’d been twenty-one, and that he’d lost almost all of it and learned more from that than from anything he’d won since.

“That’s a very convenient thing to say once you’re rich.”

“Would you prefer I’d been born brilliant?”

“Yes.”

“Then I was born brilliant. Your turn.”

“Sixteen,” said Aurelia. “Bracelets, sold at school out of my blazer pocket. I made enough to buy a camera.” She looked down at the old ledger. “Everything at home was decided for me. What I’d study, who I’d sit beside, what I’d be. Even the things I liked were meant to be useful. So I started making things. Something ordinary, turned into something people wanted to keep. And it was mine.”

He looked at her hands. “You still do that.”

“The stones are more expensive now.”

He reached across the table and took her hand, and ran his thumb over her knuckles. “Do you regret it? Even with your mother?”

“Even with my mother,” she said. “No.”

He didn’t tell her it would all be fine. He didn’t offer to fix anything. He held her hand across the ledgers, and it was enough.

At seven minutes past two she shut the last box and stretched her arms over her head. He got up and came round the table and stood in front of her chair, and looked at her mouth.

She’d become good at noticing when he wanted to kiss her. “You’re looking at something.”

“Yes.”

He lifted his hand and ran his thumb along her lower lip, slowly, and looked at the trace of colour it had taken away.

“Your lipstick’s smudged.”

“You could kiss it off.”

“I could,” he said, and didn’t. She saw something cross his face that she hadn’t seen in it before. Not amusement. Restraint, held hard. He bent and kissed her forehead instead.

“That’s not what I wanted.”

“I know.”

“You kissed me on the dock. You’ve held my hand half the night. You’ve just touched my mouth. And you’re leaving?”

“It’s nearly three. You’re tired. When I kiss you properly,” said Chen Si, “I don’t intend to be the reason you’re late for your shop.”

He picked up his jacket. At the door she said his name, and he turned.

“Tomorrow I’m taking my own car.”

“All right.”

“And no pastries.”

“Why not?”

“They’re not dinner,” said Aurelia, and he laughed, and went.

She sat in the empty room for a minute and touched her lower lip where his thumb had been.

“Ridiculous man,” she said to nobody.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car Qian looked at him in the mirror and didn’t ask anything, which was one of the reasons Qian had lasted six years.

His phone buzzed.

Aurelia: You forgot something.

Chen Si: What?

Aurelia: Your kiss.

Chen Si: I didn’t forget it. I’m keeping it for next time.

Aurelia: You can’t keep things that belong to me.

Chen Si: I thought you liked taking things that belong to other people.

Aurelia: That’s different. I’m me.

Chen Si: Goodnight, sweetheart.

She didn’t argue with it this time.

At fourteen minutes past three, crossing the empty lobby to her own car, her phone buzzed again. A number she didn’t know.

Unknown: Congratulations on the shipment. I hear the Cantù crates arrived this morning. Beautiful work.

Unknown: I’ve been following your work for some time.

She stood still under the lobby lights and read it twice, and her face went cool and smooth, the face she used on her mother. She didn’t answer. She took a picture of the screen and sent it to Chen Si.

He was still in the car. He looked at it, and Qian, watching the mirror, saw his face change.

“Find out who owns this number. Tonight.”

“Understood.”

Somebody knew about the shipment. Somebody knew which crates. Somebody had chosen to say so to her, alone, at three in the morning, rather than to him.

Chen Si: Don’t reply to it.

Aurelia: I wasn’t going to. Do you know who it is?

Chen Si: Not yet.

Aurelia: Chen Si?

Chen Si: Yes.

Aurelia: You should have kissed me.

He looked out at the dark harbour, at the cranes on the Iron Docks standing over the water like herons.

Chen Si: I know.

He’d spent the night reading the first ledger she’d ever been allowed to touch. Somewhere in it, in a neat old hand, there was a supplier’s name that also appeared, three times, in the accounts of a property company eighty per cent owned by the Song Group. He’d thought he was looking at a theft. He was beginning to understand that the theft was the smallest part of it, and that she was already standing in the middle of the rest, whether she knew it yet or not.

chapters.title: He Never Asks Her to Win
chapters.desc: She loses a game of chess on purpose to see what he’ll do. He lays down his own king.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d play with you.”
chapters.content:
The first time Aurelia asked Chen Si to teach her chess, on the second Friday of December, he looked at her as if she’d proposed something a good deal more dangerous.

It was nearly ten at night. His office took up the top floor of a building that had once belonged to a shipping line and now belonged, in every sense that mattered, to him. Beyond the glass the city lay under a thin winter haze, the traffic moving through it like slow lit rivers. Inside there was dark wood, a low fire, cedar, and the pot of tea Qian had left on the sideboard before going home. Chen Si sat behind his desk reading a report. Aurelia stood in front of it holding a walnut box.

He finished his paragraph before he looked up. “What’s that?”

“A chess set.”

“I can see that.”

“Then your eyes are better than your manners.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “What do you want, Aurelia?”

“Teach me chess.”

“You could hire a teacher.”

“I don’t want a teacher,” said Aurelia. “I want you.”

It came out with such easy certainty that even she seemed a little startled by it. He looked at her for a moment. Then he closed the report.

She opened the box on his desk. The pieces were black jade and pale soapstone, the board inlaid walnut with thin lines of mother-of-pearl between the squares. He lifted a knight and turned it to the lamp.

“An expensive way to ask someone to spend an evening with you.”

“I thought you’d appreciate the carving.”

“I appreciate the company,” he said, without any change in his face, which somehow made it worse.

They went to the low table by the windows. He turned his cuffs back once and set out the pieces and explained them, plainly, in order. The rook, the bishop, the knight and its odd crooked jump. Then the black queen, set down in her square.

“The most powerful piece on the board. She can go in any direction, as far as she likes.”

“Naturally. She sounds like me.”

“She raises fewer objections.”

Aurelia gave him a look. He set the king down beside the queen.

“He can only move one square at a time. He’s the piece everyone’s trying to protect.”

“Even though he can’t do much?”

“Because he can’t do much.”

“That sounds like a terrible arrangement.”

“Chess is full of terrible arrangements.”

“Then why does anyone play?”

“The rules are simple,” said Chen Si. “The consequences aren’t.”

She looked at him a beat too long, and then down at the board. “Teach me how to win.”

“Is that what you want?”

“Is there another reason to play?”

“Several.” He moved a pawn. “To find out what the other person values.”

“That isn’t a reason to play. That’s a reason to manipulate someone.”

“Sometimes they’re the same thing,” he said, and she laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At first she was impatient. She wanted to move fast, to attack, to force the board into a shape she could control. He stopped her whenever she missed a threat, and only then.

“Don’t move that.”

“Why?”

“You’ll lose your bishop.”

“Then I’ll take his rook.”

“And lose your queen. Stop treating it like a battlefield.”

“Isn’t that exactly what it is?”

He didn’t answer. He moved his knight, and she frowned at the board, and he watched her frown.

He was maddeningly good at teaching. He never explained too much at once and he never touched her pieces. When she blundered he let her find the blunder. When she asked something he answered without making her feel stupid for asking. It was the patience, more than the skill, that unsettled her. She was used to people who taught her things by making quite sure she knew how much she didn’t know. He seemed content just to let her learn.

After twenty minutes she began to see the rhythm of it, the shape of his attacks, the small traps folded inside harmless-looking moves. She also began to see that she was going to lose. Not because she couldn’t learn. Because he was better, far better. He seemed to see four moves ahead without appearing to think at all.

“How long have you played?” she said.

“Since I was a boy.”

“Who taught you?”

“My father.”
