Something in his voice tightened at the end of it, so slightly that almost nobody would have heard. She heard. She didn’t ask. She moved her queen out into the open instead.

“That’s a mistake,” he said.

“Perhaps I want to make it.”

He raised his eyes. There was a question in them, and he didn’t ask it either. They played on until her side of the board was a small, orderly disaster: queen in retreat, knights cut off, a rook with nowhere useful to go. She could have dragged it out. She could have made him work for the last move. Instead she walked her king, deliberately, onto the one square where his queen could take it.

He didn’t move.

He looked at the board. Then at her. She held his eyes and waited. He knew she’d seen it. She hadn’t lost because she’d missed the threat. She’d lost on purpose, to find out what he’d do. Whether he’d correct her. Whether he’d tell her she should have seen it three moves ago. Whether he’d give her the kind, worn little comforts people handed ambitious women when they lost. You’ll get better. You can’t win every time. At least you tried. She’d heard every one of them. She didn’t want any of them from him.

Chen Si reached across the board. He didn’t take her king. He picked up his own, and laid it gently on its side.

She blinked. “What are you doing?”

“Resigning.”

“You haven’t lost. You’re winning.”

“Am I?”

“Chen Si.”

“You wanted to see what I’d do.” He put his hands on his knees. “I could take your king. I could explain where you went wrong. And then we’d have a winner. Is that what you wanted?”

Aurelia looked down at his black king lying on its side between them.

She’d spent most of her life in rooms where losing was evidence. That she was careless, unworthy, not enough. Even the people who loved her turned her failures into lessons. Her mother had never needed to raise her voice. Sometimes all Vittoria had to do was go quiet.

She touched the edge of a black square. “Do you know what happened after Vienna?”

“No.”

“I won a design prize there when I was nineteen. It was small, but it mattered to me. Eight months of work. I remember the hotel, the lights, the judges, the announcement, and thinking I’d ring my mother before anyone else.” She smiled, and it didn’t hold. “She didn’t answer. I rang again that night, and the next morning, and the day after. Nine days. No congratulations. Not one question about it. On the tenth day she rang to ask me to send a photograph of myself holding the award. Not to see it. To show somebody.”

The room seemed very quiet.

“I sent it, of course. I used to think that if I won enough, one day she’d be happy for me. Not proud, even. I wasn’t greedy. Just happy, for one minute. Then I understood she wasn’t waiting for me to win. She was waiting for me to become something she could use.” She pressed her mouth flat. “I know that sounds childish.”

“No.”

“I was old enough to see what she was doing.”

“Seeing it doesn’t stop it hurting,” said Chen Si.

She held her face together for a few seconds longer. Then her eyes filled, and it made her furious, and she turned her head away as though she could stop the tears by refusing to let him watch.

He didn’t reach for her at once. He waited until she looked back. Then he got up and came round the table and sat down beside her. Not opposite. Beside.

“I hate that I still care,” she said. “I hate that one unanswered call can make me feel fourteen.”

He looked at her hands, curled hard into her palms.

“You don’t have to hate yourself,” he said, “for wanting your mother to love you.”

That was the thing that undid her. Her face crumpled before she could stop it. He caught her chin, gently.

“Look at me.”

“I look awful.”

“You look upset.”

“That’s worse.”

“Not to me,” he said, and brushed the wet from under her eye with his thumb. Then he bent and kissed her left eyelid, and her right, slowly, as if there were no hurry anywhere in the world, as if he had nothing more important to do and never would. When she finally opened her eyes his were very close.

“May I?”

She nodded. He kissed her mouth. Carefully at first, letting her decide how near she wanted him. When she put her hand to his cheek he took her face in both hands and kissed her properly, unhurried and deep, his thumb resting by her ear, and she leaned into him with a sound she’d never in her life have allowed anyone else to hear.

When they parted she kept her forehead against his.

“Your father taught you chess,” she whispered. “What happened to him?”

His eyes went to the window. For the first time that night he seemed to be deciding whether to speak.

“He was arrested when I was fifteen. He’d done some of the things they said. Not the ones they convicted him for.” His voice stayed perfectly even. Something old and cold moved under it. “He died in custody, four months later. They said it was his heart. We were given a date, a time and a sealed report, and we didn’t see him until it was too late for anyone to look properly.”

“Chen Si.”

“I learned very early not to ask questions nobody means to answer.” He turned back to her. “I’m not telling you so you’ll feel sorry for me. And I don’t want you to think you owe me anything for it.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She took his hand. For a while neither of them said anything. The two kings lay on the board, his fallen, hers standing. She traced the line of his knuckle.

“Is that why you never ask me to win?”

“Why would I?”

“Most people do.”

“Most people aren’t me.” He lifted her hand and put his mouth to her fingers. “I know what it costs to spend your whole life proving you deserve to stay in a room. I won’t make you do it with me. You can win. You can lose. You can change your mind halfway through and walk away from the board and never play again. I’ll still want you here.”

She knew how to negotiate. Shares, routes, leverage, rooms full of men who’d decided before she opened her mouth that she was too young or too pretty to matter. This wasn’t a negotiation she knew how to win. For the first time in her life she didn’t want to.

She kissed him. This time she reached first, and kept on, and he drew her in by the waist, and she felt him smile against her mouth.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling. I’m trying to be serious.”

“Are you?”

She pulled back to glare at him. He tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Very serious,” he said gravely, and she laughed, and the room loosened round them.

He set his king upright again beside hers. “One more game?”

“Will you let me win?”

“No.”

“Will you let me lose?”

“Of course.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“To play,” said Chen Si, and she looked at him for a second and reached for the black queen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian was waiting in the outer office when he came out after midnight. Aurelia had gone twenty minutes before, taking her coat and, for reasons she declined to explain, the white pieces.

“Speak,” said Chen Si.

“The number that wrote to Miss Song. It went through three relays. The phone it started on was bought eleven days ago and used for nothing else. But it was switched on twice in the same building as a man who sat on the jury in Vienna the year she won.”

Chen Si stood very still. “Find him. Who pays him now. Who he’s met. Who he’s talked to about her.”

“Understood.”

“And her mother.”

Qian waited.

“Not her public diary. Her lunches. Who she eats with, where, and who joins the table. Six months back.”

“Quietly?”

“Quietly.”

When Qian had gone he stood at the window over the city. Somebody had been watching her. Somebody had known enough of her work to congratulate her before she’d told anyone. He didn’t intend to wait until that person decided to become more interested. There was a line between protecting her and deciding things for her. He knew where it was. He also knew he’d crossed it before tonight, and he wasn’t entirely sure he’d stepped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later he found the black jade queen on the side table by his window, where she’d left it, alone, catching the lamp. Forgotten, or not. He picked it up. It was heavier than it looked. She sounds like me. He could have sent it back with Qian. He put it in the inside pocket of his jacket instead, and kept it there. Not as a trophy. As a reminder of a woman who’d walked in asking to be taught how to win, and lost on purpose to find out whether he’d still want her afterwards.

The next night her phone lit on the dressing table while she was taking off her earrings.

Mr. Thursday: You left something in my office.

Aurelia: My dignity?

Mr. Thursday: You never brought that in with you.

Aurelia: My queen?

Mr. Thursday: Yes.

Aurelia: Keep her safe.

Mr. Thursday: I intend to.

She sat down on the bed and typed, and deleted it, and typed it again.

Aurelia: Do you know what I thought when you laid your king down?

Mr. Thursday: Tell me.

Aurelia: That I could spend the rest of my life losing games to you.

He didn’t answer at once, and she very nearly sent a joke after it to take it back.

Mr. Thursday: You wouldn’t have to lose.

Aurelia: You’d let me win?

Mr. Thursday: No. I’d play with you.

She held the phone to her chest and looked at the ceiling. She thought about the balcony and the coat. About the man who’d sat down beside her while she cried and told her she didn’t have to hate herself for it. About a boy of fifteen with a sealed report in his hands. About the black jade queen in his pocket.

And then, with a clearness that startled her, she thought: I could marry this man.

Not because he was powerful. Not because he could give her buildings, or a name, or a seat in rooms that had ignored her. Because he’d watched her lose and hadn’t looked away. Because he hadn’t tried to make her losing useful to him. Because he’d never once asked her to be Number One before he’d want her.

She wasn’t going to tell him yet. She wanted to know what the decision felt like while nobody else could hear it.

Aurelia: I want another game.

Mr. Thursday: Tomorrow?

Aurelia: Tonight.

Mr. Thursday: It’s nearly eleven. Have you eaten?

She laughed out loud, alone in her bedroom, and stood up and reached for her coat. For once she wasn’t thinking about what she had to prove. She was thinking about where she wanted to go, and she wanted to go to him.

chapters.title: Dinner on the Forty-Fourth Floor
chapters.desc: He cooks her dinner and tells her how his parents died. Then she tells him to kneel, and he does.
chapters.epigraph: “Then don’t be alone when it happens.”
chapters.content:
The camera in the private lift was there for security. Chen Si had put it in two years before, after a man followed one of his guests up from the lobby. It recorded every journey to the forty-fourth floor. It was not meant to be interesting.

On the last Friday in January, Aurelia stepped into it alone, in a black dress under a long ivory coat, with her hair pinned loosely at the back and a few strands already escaping. As the doors closed she took a lipstick out of her bag and put it on with the concentration of a woman signing for several million. She pressed her lips together. She tilted her head and checked the result in the mirrored wall. Then, as if she’d just remembered something, she leaned towards the little black lens in the corner.

“Your lift is very nosy, Mr. Chen.”

Upstairs, in his kitchen, with his sleeves turned back and a knife in his hand, Chen Si looked at the screen on the wall and smiled. He pressed the intercom.

“Would you like me to take it out?”

“No. I might need proof that you behave yourself.”

“Then I’ll leave it in.”

“Don’t look so pleased with yourself.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying plenty,” said Aurelia, and the doors opened, and he switched the screen off before she could ask him how long he’d been watching. He knew she’d ask. He knew the true answer wouldn’t improve his evening.

She stopped in the kitchen doorway.

He wasn’t wearing a suit. A dark shirt with the sleeves folded to the forearm, black trousers, his watch off and lying on the counter beside a folded cloth. A pot on the stove. On the board, a whole grouper.

“You’re cooking.”

“So it seems.”

“You know how?”

“Would you like to leave?”

“No,” said Aurelia, coming in. “I want to see whether you’re going to poison me.”

“Not tonight.”

“How reassuring.”

He put the knife down and came and took her coat. His eyes went to her mouth and stayed there for a second.

“You’ve changed your lipstick.”

“How would you know?”

“I have eyes.”

“You were watching the lift.”

“I was checking security.”

“At the exact moment I was putting on lipstick.”

“An unfortunate coincidence,” said Chen Si, and hung up her coat.

She walked round his kitchen looking at everything: ginger cut into threads fine as hair, a bowl of greens, coriander, a saucer of sliced red chilli. “What’s the occasion?”

“Dinner.”

“That isn’t an occasion.”

“It is when you haven’t eaten properly. You told me on Tuesday you’d had coffee instead of lunch three days running.”

“You remember everything.”

“Not everything.”

“What do you forget?”

“Things that don’t matter,” he said, and lifted the lid of the pot. “Come and look.”

He ladled a little broth into a small bowl for her. It was too hot. Before she could blow on the spoon, he’d bent and blown across it himself, so casually that she almost didn’t notice. Almost.

“You’re spoiling me.”

“Is that a complaint?”

“Not yet.”

“Then I’ll carry on.”

He cooked without any fuss. He seemed to know by the sound when the oil was ready, by the smell when the ginger had given up what it had. She’d only ever watched his hands sign things, and hold glasses, and move pieces that changed other men’s lives. It was strange to see them do something that harmed nobody.

“Who taught you?”

“My mother.” He turned the fish. “She liked to cook. Fish especially.”

There it was again, the small change in his voice she’d heard over the chessboard. This time she didn’t let it pass.

“Tell me about them.”

He didn’t answer for a while. Then he turned off the flame. “Come and sit down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the table by the windows with the whole city underneath them. The grouper’s skin was crisp, the flesh soft as silk. He’d made the sauce on the side, and she poured on more of it than he recommended, and he watched her do it.

“You like it stronger.”

“I like to know it’s there.”

“I thought you’d say that.”

“You’ve been studying me.”

“Would you prefer I didn’t?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t stop,” said Chen Si. Then he put down his chopsticks.

“My father was called Chen Rong. He wasn’t a good man in every way. He was proud, and difficult, and sometimes cruel to the people who worked for him. But he wasn’t the man they said he was.” His eyes went to the glass. “Fu Jianguo was his closest associate. His deputy. Fu had everything my father trusted him with: the accounts, the arrangements, the letters. By the time my father understood what Fu was doing, the evidence was already in place. Every document pointed the same way. Every witness had the same story. Everyone who might have said otherwise suddenly had a reason to stay quiet.”

“He framed him.”

“Yes. And then he took his place, and climbed from there. He’s a vice-minister now.”

He said it without raising his voice, and the anger under it was old enough to have gone hard.

“My father was arrested. His partners vanished. His friends stopped taking calls. Men who’d eaten at our table for years couldn’t remember his name. My mother sat by the telephone. She thought someone would look at the evidence properly. That if she only explained, the people in charge would listen.” He reached for his glass and didn’t drink. “He died in custody. They told her after it had already happened. When she was finally allowed to see him, she came home with his watch. It had stopped. She put it on his side of the bed and didn’t move it for six years.”

Aurelia’s fingers had closed on her napkin.

“She died alone, in that house,” said Chen Si. “She’d been ill a long time and she wouldn’t go to hospital, because she didn’t want him to come home and find nobody waiting. I was twenty. I was away, trying to get close enough to Fu to see how he’d done it. I thought I had time.” He looked at the city. “I didn’t.”

She got up and came round the table. She didn’t ask whether she could touch him. She put her hand to the side of his face, her thumb at his temple, and he shut his eyes for one second.

“She shouldn’t have died alone,” she whispered.

“No.”

“Neither should your father.”

“No.”

She bent and kissed his forehead. He caught her hand and held it against his cheek.

“I spent years thinking about what I’d do once I had enough to reach him,” he said. “Now I know. I want to watch him walk down the steps of his own building at six in the morning. No car waiting. No one to open the door. Nobody coming. I want to be there when he understands that.”

“Is that enough?”

“No. But it’s a beginning.”

She didn’t tell him revenge wouldn’t bring anybody back. He knew. She didn’t tell him to forgive, or let go, or rise above it. She had no use for pretty words that couldn’t bear the weight of what he’d just said.

“Then don’t be alone when it happens,” said Aurelia.

“You’d come?”

“Yes.”

“You don’t know what you’re agreeing to.”

“I know you want somebody beside you.”

He looked at her for a long moment, and then turned her hand over and put his mouth to the inside of her wrist, exactly where he had in her shop with the red ink on her fingers.

“What’s for pudding?” she said, when she could.

“Nothing. I wanted to see whether you’d stay without it,” he said, and she threw her napkin at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she sat on his sofa with her shoes off and her feet tucked under her and her shoulder against his. Something was on the television. Neither of them knew what. She was thinking about a stopped watch on an empty pillow. He was thinking about her hand on his face.

She reached across him for the tea. He moved it out of her reach.

“It’s hot.”

“I can see that.”

“Then wait,” he said, and blew across it, and handed it to her.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Doing what?”

“Being considerate.”

“Shall I stop?”

“No.” She put the cup down. He was looking at her mouth again. She saw him see her noticing. His arm lay along the back of the sofa behind her, and her knee was against his thigh, and she could see the faint shadow along his jaw that hadn’t been there at breakfast.

“I’m deciding whether to kiss you,” she said.

“Take your time.”

They met in the middle. It wasn’t graceful. Her hand caught his collar and his found her waist and they kissed once and parted and came back to it as if neither had ever meant to stop, and then it wasn’t careful at all. He pulled her into his lap. She went. The television turned into a distant flicker. When at last they separated she stayed where she was, close enough to feel his breath.

She looked at him. Then she put her hand flat on his chest and pushed, gently, and slid back onto the sofa and away from him.

“Chen Si.”

“Yes.”

“Get on your knees.”

His face changed. The smile went out of it, and his whole attention settled on her.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

“Is that an order?”

“Do you need it again?”

“No,” he said, and stood up off the sofa, and without taking his eyes off hers went down onto his knees on the rug in front of her.

He did it slowly. Without any hurry and without any shame. A man who made whole rooms stand up when he walked into them, kneeling at her feet, looking up at her. Her breath caught. She hadn’t known it would do that to her.

“You’re actually doing it,” she said.

“You asked.”

“You’re not going to argue?”

“Would you like me to?”

“No.”

She put her fingers in his hair. It was softer than she’d thought. She pushed it back from his forehead, and he let her, his eyes following every movement of her hand.

“Do you know why I asked?”

“Because you wanted to.”

“I wanted to know whether you would.” She touched his cheek. “I don’t want you on your knees because you think I need to feel powerful. I don’t need you to make yourself small so I’ll feel big. I wanted to see if you could give me something without making me earn it.”

He took her hand and kissed the palm.

“You don’t have to earn everything,” he said.

She bent and kissed him, and he stayed on his knees with one hand light at her waist until she’d finished, which took some time.

“Come here,” she said at last, and he rose.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bedroom was at the far end of the flat. Dark wood, pale linen, a low bed, a wall of glass. No photographs on the bedside tables. Nothing on the walls. It looked like the room of a man who had never expected anyone to stay the night.

He’d closed the door and was standing just inside it, as if he were waiting to be told where he was allowed to go.

She came to him and took his collar in both hands. “Tonight I set the terms.”

“All of them?”

“Until I say otherwise.”

“All right.”

“No guessing. No deciding what I want because you think you know me.”

“I’ll ask.”

“And if I say stop?”

“I stop.”

She looked at him for a moment, at the absolute stillness in him, and found that she believed it.

“Good,” said Aurelia.

She set the pace, and it was slow. She told him when to come closer, and when to wait, and when to look at her, and he did every one of those things as if each of them mattered more than anything he’d done all year. She made him sit on the edge of the bed while she stood between his knees. She took off his watch and laid it on the bedside table. Then his cufflinks, one and then the other. Then the ring from his right hand. She set each down separately, by itself, as if she were laying out stones.

“Counting?” he said.

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Enough,” she said, and unbuttoned his shirt, one button at a time, at her own speed, and he didn’t move to help her. She kissed the hollow of his throat and felt his breath go. He caught her waist, and didn’t draw her in until she nodded, and the care in that, from him, made her smile against his skin.

“You’re very patient tonight.”

“I’m listening.”

“Keep listening.”

He kept listening. She found out what it did to him when she drew a fingernail very slowly down the inside of his wrist, and what it did when she said his name low, by his ear, and what it did when she made him wait. She found out that he would wait as long as she liked. That the man who ran half the city’s dark could lie still under her hands and simply let her, with his eyes on her face the whole time, as if watching her was the only thing in the world he’d ever wanted to be allowed to do.

Much later, she lay against his pillows with her hair loose across them and the city lights sliding slowly over the ceiling, and traced the inside of his wrist with one finger.

“You’re still behaving,” she said.

“Is that a complaint?”

“Perhaps.”

“Then tell me what you’d prefer.”

He had a particular face for waiting on her decisions. It wasn’t passive. He wasn’t a man without wants, and she knew it better now than anyone alive. He was only leaving her the room to choose.

She took his hand. “Otherwise.”

“You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

“Then it’s my turn.”

He took both her wrists in one hand and brought them up over her head and held them there against the pillow, gently, his weight settling over her with great care.

She smiled up at him. “That’s all?”

Something changed in his eyes. The amusement was still there, but there was something underneath it now, focused and dark and patient, that she’d seen before only across a boardroom table.

“Would you like me to ask again?”

“No.”

“Then tell me if that changes.”

“I will.”

And then he wasn’t waiting for her to lead. He set the pace himself, slowly, deliberately, without any hurry at all, and she discovered that handing someone the reins could feel every bit as intimate as holding them. He found every one of the things she’d found in him, and some she hadn’t known were there, and took his time over each. When his fingers tightened on her wrists and she looked up at him, he loosened them at once.

“All right?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her forehead, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth, and she laughed.

“You’re ruining the atmosphere. You’re meant to be frightening.”

“I’ll try harder,” said Chen Si, and did, and she stopped laughing.

The rest of the night belonged to the two of them. There was no performance in it and nothing either of them had to prove. Two people who’d spent their whole lives keeping hold of everything, finding out that with the right person letting go felt safe.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke just before dawn and didn’t know the ceiling. Then she felt the warmth beside her and turned.

He was lying on his side with one arm under the pillow, watching her.

“Good morning,” he said.

“How long have you been awake?”

“Not long.”

“Liar.”

He reached past her for the glass of water on the bedside table before she could, and handed it to her. Beside the glass stood a small black velvet box. She opened it. The black jade queen lay inside on the velvet.

“You’ve had this six weeks.”

“Yes.”

“You carried it about?”

“Not everywhere.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“You told me to keep her safe.”

“I was joking.”

“I wasn’t,” said Chen Si.

She turned the queen in the early light. Then she put it down by the glass and leaned over and kissed him, sleepily, her hand along his jaw.

“Keep her.”

“I thought you wanted her back.”

“I do. Keep her till I ask. And the next time we play, I’m winning.”

“I’d expect nothing less.”

“Don’t let me.”

“I won’t.”

She shut her eyes, smiling. Outside the glass the city was waking. Inside, a man who’d learned as a boy to wait for a telephone that never rang was lying beside a woman who’d chosen to stay.

At seventeen minutes past eight Qian’s phone buzzed.

Chen Si: Move the nine o’clock to eleven. And send up breakfast.

Qian read it twice. In six years Chen Si had never moved a meeting for an extra hour in bed.

Qian: For one, or two?

There was a short pause.

Chen Si: Two.

Qian didn’t smile. He did ring the kitchen and order breakfast for two, and the eggs the way he’d once heard Miss Song ask for them at the Jade Hall.

On the forty-fourth floor Aurelia had gone back to sleep, one hand lying near the black queen. Chen Si drew the blanket up over her shoulder. He’d spent six weeks carrying a chess piece about because handing it back would have meant admitting he wanted a reason to see her. Now she was here. And for once in his life, he had no intention of making the next move.

chapters.title: A Proposal With Terms and Conditions
chapters.desc: She proposes with eleven pages of red ink. He signs every one, and writes something in the margin she can’t argue with.
chapters.epigraph: “Not everything has to be perfect to be worth keeping.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past ten on Tuesday the twelfth of March, a girl from Aurelia’s shop delivered a cream envelope to the top floor of Chen Holdings, put it into Chen Si’s own hands, and refused to answer a single question. It was sealed with dark red wax. On the front, in her hand, it said Mr. Chen Si and nothing else.

Dear Mr. Chen,

You are required to attend a meeting at my shop at 11:30 this morning. Attendance is compulsory. Please bring a pen.

You may bring a lawyer. I reserve the right to send him away if he becomes irritating.

Aurelia Song

He read it twice and looked up. “Cancel the half past eleven.”

“That’s the shipping consortium,” said Qian. “They’ve waited three weeks.”

“Then they can wait a fourth.” He folded the letter into his inside pocket, beside the black jade queen. “And find me a pen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was quiet when he came in at twenty-nine minutes past. Spring sun through the tall windows. The new collection along the far wall under soft light, emeralds and white diamonds and necklaces that looked like water caught in the act of freezing. It was still hers, every inch. The name over the door. The staff. The books. He could have bought the whole building without noticing the cost, and he’d never once put his name anywhere in it.

She was behind the centre counter in an ivory suit with her hair swept back and a deep red mouth, looking extremely pleased with herself. In front of her was a stack of paper. A thick one.

“You’re late,” she said.

“It’s eleven twenty-nine.”

“Late by my standards.”

“Then I apologise to your standards.” He sat down opposite her. “Am I being interviewed?”

“Negotiated with.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Very,” said Aurelia, and slid the first page across to him.

At the top, in black capitals, it said: PROPOSED MARRIAGE AGREEMENT.

He didn’t move. He read the line again. She watched him with an expression of perfect composure, and her fingertips were pressed white against the edge of the glass.

“Is this a joke?” he said.

“No.”

“An acquisition?”

“Not unless you’re offering yourself as an asset.”

“You’re proposing.”

“I’m proposing a legally and emotionally sensible arrangement with a view to marriage.”

“How romantic.”

“I knew you’d appreciate the language.”

There were eleven pages, all in her hand, with clauses underlined in red and amendments climbing up the margins.

“How long did this take?”

“Long enough.”

“Did you sleep?”

“That isn’t relevant.”

“It is if you were drafting marriage contracts at three in the morning.”

“Are you going to read it,” said Aurelia, “or interrogate me?”

“Both,” said Chen Si, and read.

Clause One. Both parties enter freely, without pressure, debt or fear, and neither gives up who they are. Neither may use the marriage to take control of the other’s business. Her shop, her designs, her staff, her collections and every future one remain hers alone.

“You’ve specified that I may not appoint myself chairman.”

“You’re not funny.”

“It seemed worth checking.”

Clause Two, separate property. Three, what they’d own together. Four: each keeps their own friends, their own hours, and one room the other doesn’t enter without knocking. Five: neither family has any say in their house. Six, the press, and the right to refuse every interview ever asked for. Seven: the money, all of it, open to both. Eight: what’s private stays private.

He turned the page, and stopped.

Clause Nine. Private terms.

Within the marriage, intimacy is under the Wife’s direction until she says otherwise. Nothing is owed because of the marriage. Nothing is assumed. Silence is never consent. The terms may change only by agreement.

He read it twice. “Until you say otherwise.”

“Yes.”

“And if you never do?”

“Then you’ll have a very peaceful marriage.”

“That seems unlikely.”

“Don’t be arrogant.”

“I’m being optimistic.”

She leaned in. “Do you object?”

“No,” said Chen Si. “Not at all.”

Clause Ten. The word.

The word is Milan. When either party says it, everything stops at once, without argument, without penalty, and without any demand to explain. Either party may stop anything at any time.

“Milan,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Not Rotterdam?”

“Rotterdam is reserved for Rotterdam.”

He laughed, low.

“Don’t laugh. It’s a serious clause.”

“I know it is,” he said, and stopped laughing, and read it once more, slowly.

Clause Eleven. Choice.

Neither party stays because of reputation, family, money or fear. The marriage continues only as long as both choose it. After ten years it ends, unless it is renewed; at the renewal the Wife may rewrite every clause.

He put the pages down on the glass. For a few seconds he said nothing at all, and the composure on her face began, very slightly, to slip.

“Well?”

“Where’s the proposal?”

She blinked. “What?”

“You’ve given me eleven pages of terms. Where’s the part where you ask me to marry you?”

“That’s what this is.”

“I know what it is. I want to hear you say it.”

For all her preparation and all her careful clauses, she hadn’t prepared for this. She looked down at the contract and back up at him.

“Chen Si.”

“Yes.”

“I want to marry you.” She went on before she could lose her nerve. “Not for your name. Not for protection. Not because you can make things disappear. Because I want you in my life. I want to wake up next to you, and argue with you at breakfast, and steal your food, and complain about how little you sleep. I want to know what you look like at seventy, still trying to tell everybody what to do.”

“At seventy I may have more authority.”

“You’ll have less hair.”

“That’s cruel.”

“You’re welcome.” Her face changed, became serious. “I want to choose you. But I don’t want to disappear into your life to do it.”

He reached across the counter and took her hand.

“You won’t.”

“Don’t promise what you can’t control.”

“Then I won’t.” He brought her fingers to his mouth. “I’ll promise to notice if you start to disappear. And to listen when you tell me I’m the reason.”

“That’s acceptable.”

“Good. Where’s the pen?”

She pushed a black fountain pen towards him. He signed the first page, and the second, and the third. He didn’t ask for any change to the money, or the business, or the family. At Clause Nine he stopped just long enough to read it once more, and signed. At Ten, he signed. At the end he turned the last page over and wrote on the back of it, in black, under her red, for some time. Then he slid it back to her.

Additional disclosure. I have been in love with Aurelia Song since the night on the balcony when she would not cry in front of me. She has never needed to win, impress anyone, or become anything else to deserve it. I am choosing her exactly as she is.

Chen Si

She read it three times.

“You can’t put that in a contract.”

“Why not?”

“It isn’t an obligation.”

“Then it’s a disclosure. Can you argue with it?”

She looked at the paper. “No.”

“Good.”

“Since the balcony?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“At first because I thought you’d leave.” He turned the pen in his fingers. “Later, because I wanted you to know me well enough to decide whether you could love me without the information. I didn’t want you to feel you owed me an answer.”

“That was very unfair.”

“I know.”

She took the pen out of his hand and signed the last page. Aurelia Song.

“There.”

“That’s it?”

“That’s it.”

“We’re engaged.”

“We’re engaged.”

“Should I buy you a ring?”

She looked offended. “Are you suggesting I haven’t already considered the matter?”

“Have you?”

“Obviously.”

“Then I won’t interfere,” said Chen Si, and stood up, and for a moment stayed on his side of the counter just looking at her, like a man who’d been handed something he’d not allowed himself to want. Then he came round it.

“Mr. Chen. You’re crossing a boundary.”

“I believe the contract allows it.”

“With notice.”

He stopped in front of her. “May I?”

“Yes,” said Aurelia.

It wasn’t a restrained kiss. His hand came up to her face, his thumb at the edge of her mouth, and she took a fistful of his shirt and pulled him down, and forgot the contract and Lily in the back with the trays and the front door that nobody had locked. When he lifted his head his mouth was red with her lipstick, and she looked at it and laughed.

“Your fault,” he said.

“You came round the counter.”

“You invited me.”

“I didn’t invite you to ruin my lipstick.”

“Shall I apologise?”

“Not yet,” she said, and he kissed her again, carefully this time, and she smiled against his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the last client had gone she took something out of the drawer under the counter and put it in his hand. A thin gold chain, a little dulled, with a small pendant. One link had parted near the clasp.

“It broke,” she said.

“So I see.”

“It was in the window. Bottom left, beside the pearl earrings. It was there the morning you walked in with your letter, and every day after that while my mother was trying to close me down. It wasn’t the most expensive thing I had. It wasn’t the cleverest. I just liked it.” She touched it in his palm. “I want you to have it. It isn’t a wedding present. Don’t be dramatic.”

“I wasn’t going to be.”

“You were thinking about it.”

“I was thinking that you kept something broken instead of throwing it away.”

“Not everything has to be perfect to be worth keeping.”

His fingers closed over it. “I’ll have the chain mended.”

“No. Leave it as it is.”

He looked at the parted link a moment longer, and nodded, and put it in his pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven she locked the door and turned off the window lights and walked once through the dark shop, the way she did every night. Then she put the contract in a leather folder and held it out to him.

“Your copy. Qian can make another.”

“I don’t need another. Keep it.”

“You’re trusting me with the only signed copy?”

“I trust you with a good deal more than that.”

“Such as?”

“Me,” said Chen Si.

She reached for his tie. “Come upstairs.”

The workroom over the shop was smaller than his office: a long bench against one wall under a lamp, a sofa by the window, sketches pinned to a board, half-made pieces lying in velvet trays waiting for hands. She put the folder on the desk and took a length of black silk out of a drawer.

“Is that part of the contract?” he said.

“Not exactly.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Would you like to be?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then give me your hands.”

He held them out. She brought his wrists together and wound the silk round them twice and tied it loosely, in a knot one tug would undo. Then she checked it the way she checked a setting.

“Comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Too tight?”

“No.”

“Fingers?”

He moved them. “Yes.”

“Are you nervous?” she asked.

“You’re the one asking all the questions,” he said. “I’m the one who’s tied up.”

She’d imagined this before. Not the details. The feeling: the man who commanded rooms standing perfectly still because she’d asked him to. Because he trusted her to hold the thing without dropping it.

“Look at me,” she said, and he did. “Clause Nine?”

“Every word.”

“Ten?”

“Milan.”

She kissed him, and he didn’t move his hands. She stepped in close with her palm flat on his chest and took her time, deciding when to kiss him and when to stop and when to run one fingertip along his jaw, and he followed her lead with a patience that made her feel powerful and treasured both at once. She unbuttoned his shirt herself. She took his tie off and dropped it on the bench. She found the place below his ear that made him close his eyes, and stayed there until his breathing was no longer quite steady, and he still didn’t move his hands.

Then she drew back.

“Chen Si.”

“Yes.”

“Otherwise.”

His eyes changed. “You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

“Say it.”

“Yes. I want you to.”

He pulled the knot loose with one tug and the silk fell, and he took her hand and kissed the inside of her wrist, and then he drew her in. His hands went to her waist and her back. He lifted her onto the edge of the workbench and stopped there, with her face in his hands, to be sure she was comfortable.

“You’re very careful,” she said.

“I’ve got something valuable in my hands.”

“That’s a terrible line.”

“Did it work?”

She pulled him closer by his open shirt. “Unfortunately.”

He laughed against her mouth. The bench stopped being a place for sketches. The papers went to one side and the lamp stayed on, low, and the rest of the night was theirs. There was no contest in it about who held more. She’d given him the lead and he took it the way he’d taken her terms, attentively, watching her face, listening to every answer, and never mistaking permission once given for permission for good. When she drew him closer, he came. When she told him to wait, he waited, though it cost him, and she could see that it did, and that he would have gone on waiting as long as she asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly midnight when she spoke again, lying against his chest on the sofa with one hand over his heart. Her lipstick was gone and her hair was ruined and there was a faint red line round his wrist where the silk had been.

“Are you happy?”

“Yes.”

“Even with eleven pages of conditions?”

“Because of eleven pages of conditions.”

“You’re going to regret it.”

“Probably. I’ll regret a great many things,” he said. “Marrying you won’t be one of them.”

She hid her face in his shoulder. “Good.”

After a while he took the small velvet box out of his jacket on the floor and opened it. The black jade queen.

“You kept her,” said Aurelia.

“You told me to keep her until you asked. You haven’t asked.” He put the piece into her palm and closed her fingers round it. “But I think she belongs with you now.”

“You carried her because I lost the game on purpose.”

“I carried her because you wanted to see what I’d do.”

“And now I know,” she said, and looked down at the black queen in her hand. “I can lose a game and still be loved.”

“You could lose a thousand,” said Chen Si.

She kissed him and lay back down on him with the queen shut in her fist. On the bench beside them the eleven pages lay in their folder, red ink and black. Terms for money and privacy and family and the boundaries of their nights, and a clause for the day they might choose to stop choosing. And on the back of the last page, in his hand, one paragraph she had tried for an entire morning to argue with, and couldn’t, and for once in her life hadn’t wanted to.

chapters.title: The Song Parents Are Not Told
chapters.desc: She marries him in Milan with eleven guests and the sister she hasn’t spoken to in two years, and her mother finds out from a magazine.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you’re already late.”
chapters.content:
At thirteen minutes past two on the morning of his wedding, in a hotel above the Navigli, Chen Si was learning to say I promise in Italian. He had been learning for thirty-seven nights. On the other end of the line, in Aurelia’s workshop on the far side of the world, Enzo sounded profoundly unimpressed.

“Again.”

“Lo prometto.”

“No. You sound as though you’re threatening somebody.”

“I’m making a promise.”

“Then sound like a man making a promise and not a man collecting a debt.”

Chen Si shut his eyes. “Lo prometto.”

“Better.”

“Good.”

“Not good. Better. There is a difference, and it is my whole life’s work.” Enzo sighed down the line. “God give me patience. Now the vows.”

He’d written them himself. He’d refused the hotel’s translator, refused the planner’s suggestion that the ceremony be held in English, refused to let anyone else put words in his mouth for her. His Italian wasn’t good. His pronunciation was painstaking. His meaning was not in doubt.

“You understand all of it?” said Enzo.

“Enough.”

“Marriage isn’t a business agreement, you know.”

Chen Si looked at the handwritten page on the desk. “Have you met my fiancée?”

Enzo laughed out loud. “Ah. Then perhaps you’re right to bring a contract.”

“She wrote eleven pages. In red.”

“Then marry her quickly before she adds a twelfth.” A pause, and a gentler voice. “Your mother. Would she have liked this?”

Chen Si looked out over the dark canal for a while.

“She’d have corrected my pronunciation.”

“Good woman. Go to sleep. You’re getting married tomorrow.”

“Today.”

“Then you’re already late,” said Enzo, and rang off.

At the bottom of the page, under the Italian, Chen Si had written one more sentence, in his own language. He wouldn’t need anyone to teach him how to say that one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was still up in the next room when he went through, in a silk robe in front of the mirror, with the dress hanging behind her. Ivory, clean-lined, almost architectural, with hand-sewn work along the neckline and nothing else. No train. No acres of lace. Nothing to make her look like anybody but herself. She’d chosen every inch of it.

“You’re awake,” he said.

“So are you. Who was that?”

“Business.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

He came and stood behind her with his hands at her waist, and they looked at the two of them together in the glass.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Today.”

“Don’t correct me the night before my wedding.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Did you? Did you eat? What have you been practising?”

He went perfectly still. Her eyes narrowed in the mirror.

“Go to bed, Aurelia,” said Chen Si, and kissed her shoulder, and she let him steer her there, deeply suspicious, and didn’t find out about the Italian until the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding had eleven guests. That was deliberate. She’d refused a ballroom, a procession of associates, a guest list that turned a marriage into a map of alliances. She wanted the people who mattered and nobody else, and Chen Si had agreed without one word of argument.

Zhao came first, alone, in a dark suit, with a small parcel in plain paper. He bowed his head to her.

“Mrs. Chen.”

“Not yet.”

“Then I’ll practise.”

Inside was a plum blossom carved from white jade. “For the new house,” he said, and that was all, no blessing, no speech about duty. Only the plain approval of a man who’d watched her earn it.

Qian, with his wife on his arm, brought Chen Si’s mother’s recipe book, wrapped in linen, and put it in his hands without a word of explanation. Chen Si held it for some time.

Then Enzo, red-eyed already, who’d flown in the night before and had been on the telephone till two. Lily. Two old friends from Milan. Old Fan, in a suit nobody had known he owned. The two men from the Jade Hall Chen Si trusted most.

There was one person missing, and Aurelia was not waiting for her. She checked the courtyard door three times and her phone twice, and told the planner each time that everything was going exactly as intended.

Twenty minutes before the ceremony, the door opened.

Her sister was standing in it, in a blue dress with a grease mark on one knuckle she’d obviously tried and failed to scrub off, holding white flowers in a fist.

“Serafina.”

They hadn’t properly spoken in two years. Birthdays gone by without a call. Messages unanswered. One ugly argument, in a kitchen in the house on the Peak, that had ended with Aurelia saying something unforgivable and Serafina refusing to forgive it. They’d grown up in the same house, under the same rules, surviving the same mother, and they’d learned to survive in opposite ways. Serafina had got loud and walked out. Aurelia had got sharp and stayed. Somewhere between them the silence had grown too wide to cross.

“You came,” said Aurelia.

Serafina’s eyes were already wet. “Of course I came, you idiot.”

“I didn’t know whether you would.”

“I didn’t know whether you’d want me.”

“I did,” said Aurelia, too fast for it to be anything but true.

Serafina put the flowers down on a chair and crossed the room and held on to her. Neither of them said anything for a while.

“I’m sorry,” Serafina whispered.

“So am I.”

“I should have rung.”

“I should have answered.”

“You always had to be the one who walked away first.”

“And you always waited for me to come back.”

“Someone had to,” said Serafina, and Aurelia laughed with her forehead pressed against her sister’s.

Serafina took an envelope out of her bag. In it was a photograph: two small girls in front of a shop window in Milan, the elder in a paper crown gone crooked, looking at the camera as if it had personally disappointed her, with one arm round the younger, who was holding up a plastic necklace and grinning with every tooth she had.

“Where did you find this?”

“Your old room. You kept it in your maths book.”

“Will you stay?”

“Today. Tomorrow. As long as you want.”

Across the room Chen Si watched them and didn’t come closer. Some things couldn’t be mended by somebody standing nearby with good intentions. When Serafina finally looked over at him he inclined his head, and after a moment she returned it.

“He keeps looking at you,” she murmured.

“He always does.”

“Good,” said Serafina, and picked her flowers back up.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the little room off the courtyard where the groom was meant to wait, Zhao checked the rings for the third time and put the box back in his pocket and patted it.

“Your hands are shaking,” he said.

Chen Si looked down at them. They were. He hadn’t noticed. They hadn’t shaken in the drain at sixteen, or in the room where they’d read him his father’s report, or on any of the nights since when it would have been reasonable.

“It’s warm in here,” he said.

“It’s May. It’s cold in here.” Zhao leaned on the wall with his arms folded and the strand of hair that never stayed falling over one eye. “You can still run. I’d drive.”

“I know you would.”

“I’d tell her it was my fault.”

“She wouldn’t believe you.”

“No,” Zhao agreed. “She’s not stupid. That’s the trouble with her.” He looked at the floor for a while. “Si.”

“Yes.”

“She sat in your chair.”

“I know. I was watching.”

“I’d have sat on the floor.” Zhao straightened up off the wall and did up his jacket, which he never did. “Your mother would have fed her till she couldn’t move. Come on. You’ll be late, and then she’ll put it in a clause.”

Chen Si laughed, the short unwilling one that only two people alive could get out of him, and went out into the courtyard with his brother a step behind him and his hands, for the moment, still.

✦ ✦ ✦

The palazzo stood on the bank of the canal, its stone face elegant rather than grand, its inner courtyard full of pale roses and the smell of orange blossom. No crowd outside. Nobody from the Song house. She’d made that decision herself, and he hadn’t tried to change it.

Zhao stood beside Chen Si as best man and looked faintly uncomfortable about it.

“You’re not nervous?” Aurelia whispered on her way past.

“I’ve negotiated with men a great deal more difficult than a wedding.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

Then she saw Chen Si by the table in a black suit, and for one rare moment his composure went. His eyes softened. His lips parted. He seemed to forget there was anyone else in the courtyard.

She’d carried small flowers, white garden roses, so as not to hide her hands. When she reached him he took her fingers and ran his thumb over the place the ring would go.

“Beautiful,” he said.

“You’re biased.”

“Completely.”

The vows were in Italian. Hers she’d practised with Enzo, and she said them carefully, her accent still a little Milanese after all these years. She promised to choose him freely, to tell him the truth, and to guard the life they built without giving up the woman she’d been before him.

Then Chen Si took both her hands and began.

His Italian wasn’t flawless. It was deliberate. He looked straight at her the whole way through. He promised not to mistake her independence for distance. Not to treat her love as something bought or earned by keeping her safe. Not to make her decisions for her and call it care. To listen when she told him he was wrong. To keep choosing her. And at the end of it, low, in his own language, the one sentence nobody had taught him: Wherever you stand, I’ll stand beside you.

Enzo was crying openly. Aurelia was staring.

“You learned all that?”

“Every night.”

“From Enzo?”

“Unfortunately,” said Chen Si, and Enzo made a small offended noise, and she laughed, and the tears she’d been holding all day went over at last.

The rings went on. Hers was a narrow line of diamonds in platinum, made to sit beside the stone she’d chosen in March and not compete with it. She’d designed it. He’d approved it. Nothing about it had been decided without her. When they were pronounced married he lifted her hand and kissed her ring finger, and then kissed her mouth, warm and certain and long enough that Zhao cleared his throat.

“Mine,” he murmured against her lips.

“Careful.”

“By your own contract.”

“Which clause?”

“Nine.”

She laughed and touched his cheek. “Yours by choice.”

His face changed. He kissed her again, and this time nobody interrupted.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were only a few photographs. The two of them under the old stone arch. Aurelia laughing while Chen Si tried and failed to straighten her veil. Zhao beside them with the grave face of a man given an unfamiliar duty he meant to discharge correctly. And one of the sisters alone by the water, Aurelia laughing and Serafina looking at her, neither of them aware of the camera. That was the one Aurelia kept.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight forty-two that evening, in the house on the Peak, Vittoria Conti Song found out that her elder daughter was married.

Not by telephone. Not by invitation. Not from some relative who’d decided she ought to be told. From Gilt, whose evening edition had put out a short feature with photographs from a palazzo courtyard.

A Private Wedding in Milan: Aurelia Song Marries Chen Si.

Aurelia beside him with her hand flat on his chest, her ring catching the light, smiling at him and not at the camera. Eleven guests. A mention of her label. A mention of his investments. A mention of the bride’s sister, Serafina, who had attended.

No mention of Vittoria at all. No quotation. No family portrait. No sign anywhere that the bride had grown up in the Song house.

She read it twice. She had a coffee cup in her hand, the thin old porcelain from her own mother’s set, and her fingers closed on it, and it made a small sharp sound, and a crack ran up its side.

She put it down very carefully.

“How long has this been known?”

The secretary across the desk didn’t answer at once.

“How long?”

“I don’t know, madam.”

“Find out,” said Vittoria, and picked up her phone, and looked at her daughter’s name on it for a long moment, and pressed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Milan, at the long table under the arches, Aurelia’s phone lit up beside her plate.

Mother.

Serafina saw the name and her face went still. Chen Si saw it too. He didn’t reach for the phone. He didn’t tell her what to do. He went on talking to Enzo and left the choice where it belonged.

The phone stopped ringing. A moment later, a message.

Vittoria: I see you have married.

Then another.

Vittoria: You might have informed your family.

Under the table Serafina’s hand found hers.

Aurelia read them both again. She thought about the balcony, and the nine days after Vienna, and a toast that had closed her shop between the canapés and the cake. She thought about a little girl in a paper crown who’d believed that if she won enough, one day her mother would look at her the way mothers looked at children in films.

Then she looked at Chen Si, who was still talking to Enzo with his hand lying loose on the table an inch from hers, not asking her for anything.

She turned the phone face down.

“Are you all right?” said Serafina.

“Yes,” said Aurelia, and found, a little to her own astonishment, that it was true. “Actually,” she said, “I’m married.”

Serafina laughed. “Yes, you are.”

Across the table Chen Si glanced up. Aurelia lifted her left hand and turned it so the ring caught the lamps. He reached over, took it, and kissed the backs of her fingers, and went on with his conversation as if nothing at all had happened, and kept hold of her hand.

chapters.title: Blood Brothers at the Reception
chapters.desc: Zhao makes a nine-word speech and Serafina offers her a getaway car. On the wedding night, the bride blindfolds her husband with her veil.
chapters.epigraph: “He is my brother. You’re his. So you’re family.”
chapters.content:
By the time the last course had gone, Zhao Zhendong had decided he would not be making a speech. He’d told Chen Si so twice. The first time Chen Si had nodded. The second time he’d said, “You don’t have to,” and Zhao had looked at him for several seconds and said, “Good.”

Now he was on his feet at the long table under the arches with a glass in his hand, and all eleven guests were looking at him.

“Did you arrange this?” Aurelia murmured.

“No,” said Chen Si, with one arm along the back of her chair.

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m allowed to smile at my wedding. I’m enjoying his suffering.”

Zhao cleared his throat. “I don’t make speeches.”

“We know,” said Aurelia.

“I don’t think a marriage needs a room to approve it.”

“Also true.”

Zhao looked down the table at Chen Si. He’d met him at fifteen, in a place neither of them ever named at dinner. He’d seen him as a boy who didn’t speak for a month, and as a young man who kept his grief where nobody could reach it, and as the man who’d built a kingdom out of what was left of his father’s ruin. He’d stood beside him through things that couldn’t be told at any table. And now there he sat, looking at the woman next to him as if the rest of the courtyard had become a detail.

Zhao lifted his glass.

“He is my brother. You’re his. So you’re family.”

Nine words. He said them without any ceremony at all, and drank.

Nobody spoke for a moment. Aurelia looked at him across the candles. She knew what it was to be claimed by a family, and she knew what it was to be shut out of one. This wasn’t either. He wasn’t handing her a place somebody had prepared for her. He was telling her that the place was hers because Chen Si had chosen her, and because Zhao had decided, on his own, to choose her too.

She lifted her glass. “Then I suppose I should say thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

“That was nine words,” said Chen Si.

“Don’t count them,” said Zhao, and sat down, and Chen Si reached under the table and took his wife’s hand.

Enzo blew his nose. At the far end of the table Serafina looked at Zhao for a long, considering moment, like a woman revising an opinion she’d brought with her from the airport, and then lifted her glass to him as well. Old Fan, who’d understood only that a young man had stood up and said something short and true, slapped the table twice with his palm in loud approval.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina found her by the fountain at the far end of the courtyard, where a small bronze figure stood in a basin of pale stone with the water running quietly off its shoulders. Aurelia had taken off her shoes and was holding them by the straps, walking barefoot on the cool flags.

“You’re escaping your own wedding.”

“I’m taking a break from being admired. It’s exhausting.”

Serafina handed her a glass of water and stood beside her. Somewhere behind them Chen Si’s voice, low and even, talking to Zhao.

“He looks at you a lot,” said Serafina. “Even when he’s talking to someone else.”

“He’s easily distracted.”

“Can I say something? And you won’t think I’m trying to ruin your wedding.”

Aurelia’s face changed. “All right.”

“I don’t trust him. Not all the way.” Serafina looked at the water in her glass. “I know who he is. I know what people say about him, and that he can make things happen without anyone ever finding out he was there.”

“Some of what they say is true.”

“That’s what worries me.” She lowered her voice. “If you ever need to leave, I’ve got a car. A driver I’d trust with my life, which I have, at two hundred an hour, more than once. Wherever you are. Whenever. You ring, it comes. No questions.”

Aurelia stared at her.

“I don’t want you staying just because you married him,” said Serafina. “Or because everybody knows. Or because leaving would be complicated. You spent your whole life being told to put up with things because you were already in the room. I don’t want you doing it again.”

“You brought me a getaway car for a wedding present.”

“I thought it was practical.”

“It’s a terrible present.”

“I can get you something else.”

“No.” Aurelia put her glass on the edge of the basin and took her sister’s hand. “It’s a very good present. I’ll remember it.”

“Even if you never use it?”

“Even then.”

“Do you love him?”

Aurelia looked back across the courtyard. Chen Si had turned, and his eyes found her at once. He didn’t call her. He only looked, and waited.

“Yes,” she said. And then again, more quietly, as if checking it against something. “I love him. Not because he can protect me. Because when I’m with him I don’t have to perform. I can be difficult and unreasonable, I can lose a game or sit in a corner and say nothing all night, and he doesn’t make me earn it. He lets me be a person.”

Serafina squeezed her hand. “Then I’m happy for you.”

“Let’s not waste another two years.”

“Agreed.”

They held on to each other by the fountain with the water running behind them, and when they let go Serafina said, “He’s coming. Remember the car.”

Chen Si stopped beside them. “Am I interrupting?”

“Yes,” said Serafina.

“Should I go?”

“No,” said Aurelia. “You’re my husband.”

He held out his hand. “Then may I have my wife?”

“Take her,” said Serafina. “But give her back.”

He looked at her quite seriously. “Always.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after ten the musicians began a slow waltz.

“I’ve lost my shoes,” said Aurelia.

He looked at the shoes hanging from her fingers. “How unfortunate.”

He took them off her, held them by the straps in one hand, and gave her the other, and walked her out under the lights. One hand at her waist. Her shoes swinging gently from the other.

“You’re holding my shoes like a handbag.”

“I’ve held worse.”

“Don’t say that while holding my wedding shoes.”

“Shall I put them down?”

“No.”

“Then stop complaining,” said Chen Si, and she laughed into his shoulder.

They turned slowly under the arches. “Your best man made a speech,” she said.

“An unfortunate development.”

“Do you know what I liked? He didn’t say I belonged to you. He said I was yours, and so now I’m his family too. And he meant every word of it.”

“He did.”

She looked at his mouth. He saw her do it.

“What?”

“I’m allowed to look.”

She came up on her toes, and he met her halfway, in the middle of the waltz, his hand firm at her waist and her fingers curled into his shoulder, and the guests applauded and Enzo whistled, and when he lifted his head her shoes were still hanging from his fingers.

“Remarkable,” she said.

“I haven’t dropped them,” said Chen Si, and kissed her again, and this time didn’t care in the least who was watching.

✦ ✦ ✦

Their rooms looked over the canal. She stood at the open window with the water dark under the old stone bridge, and he came and gave her a glass of water and stood beside her, and for a while neither of them said anything.

“You arranged the photographs,” she said.

He didn’t answer at once.

“Don’t pretend.”

“I made sure a photographer knew there was a wedding.”

“You planted him.”

“I arranged for him to be there.”

“So that my mother would find out.”

A pause. “Yes. I wanted her to learn that you’d married without being given the chance to make the day about herself.”

“That was mine to decide.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you decide it?”

His jaw tightened. “Because I wanted to protect the day.”

It wasn’t an unreasonable answer. It wasn’t an acceptable one either. She turned to face him.

“You could have asked me. You could have told me. You decided. I don’t want my marriage to be one more thing people arrange around me. Not my mother. Not my husband.”

His face changed at the word. Husband.

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

“I’m learning,” said Chen Si.

She looked at him for some time. Then she took his hand. “Don’t make me sorry I gave you the right to stand beside me.”

“I won’t.”

“That’s a promise?”

“Lo prometto,” he said, carefully, and she heard Enzo in it and very nearly laughed, and didn’t.

“Are you sorry?” he said. “That you didn’t invite her?”

“No.” She thought about it properly. “I’m sorry that I wanted her there. That’s the part I have to live with. I wanted my mother to watch me get married and think I’d done something beautiful. I just didn’t want it enough to let her take the day away from me.”

“That makes sense.”

“Good,” said Aurelia, and leaned on him, and he rested his cheek on her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her jewellery off for her at the mirror, one piece at a time, the earrings and the bracelet and the pins from her hair. The rings stayed. Then he stood behind her with his hands at her waist.

“Does it feel strange?” she said. “Being married?”

“No. I’ve wanted it for a long time.”

“How long?”

“Since the balcony.”

“You’re very consistent.”

“I’ve had a clear objective.”

He bent to kiss her. She let him, and then drew back. “Wait.”

He stopped at once.

She picked up the veil from the dressing table, a long fall of ivory tulle with a border of hand embroidery, and folded it in her hands.

“Do you trust me?”

“Yes.”

“Then turn round.”

He turned. She laid the folded tulle over his eyes and tied it loosely behind his head.

“Can you see?”

“No.”

“Uncomfortable?”

“No.”

“Can you breathe?”

“Yes, Aurelia.”

She came round in front of him. It was very nearly absurd: Chen Si, who could make old men lower their voices by walking into a room, standing in the middle of their wedding suite blindfolded with a piece of her veil. She touched his jaw.

“You’re very obedient.”

“Tonight.”

“Don’t spoil it.”

She took a fine gold chain from her jewellery case, one of her own, light enough to move and strong enough to hold its shape, and looped it once round both his wrists. Not a lock. A promise any movement could undo. She checked it as she’d check a clasp.

“What would you like me to do?” he said.

“Nothing yet.”

He smiled under the veil.

“Do you know what I like about you? You’re never frightened when I take control.”

“I know you.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he agreed. “I know you won’t take what you haven’t been given.”

She kissed his cheek, and his jaw, and the corner of his mouth, and he didn’t follow her. He stood and waited, and she kissed him properly, and still he didn’t move his hands.

“Do you remember the first time you called me sweetheart?”

“Yes.”

“You sounded far too pleased with yourself.”

“I was.”

“And now?”

He turned his head towards her voice. “Now I have a wife.”

“That’s not an answer.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“My queen,” said Chen Si.

She went still. He hadn’t said it to tease. He hadn’t said it to provoke a smile. My queen.

“Again.”

“My queen.”

“That’s the first time.”

“I know.”

“Why now?”

“Because today you stood next to me and didn’t give up one single piece of yourself to do it.”

“And that makes me a queen?”

“No,” he said. “You were one before I met you. I’m only the first man who’s said so.”

Her throat closed. She slid the chain off his wrists and untied the veil, and when he opened his eyes she was looking at him with an expression he’d almost never seen on her. Not confidence. Not amusement. Something much quieter.

“Come here,” he said, and she went.

The rest of the night went slowly. She laid the veil by their rings on the dressing table. He helped her out of the layers of her dress, button by button, stopping whenever she told him to and starting only when she said so, and she kissed him between small instructions, and laughed when he misunderstood one of them on purpose, and stopped laughing when he stopped misunderstanding. There was no audience now. No family watching, nothing to negotiate. The water moved under the window, and the city went quiet, and the night they’d chosen for themselves was theirs from end to end.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest, turning his wedding ring round and round on his finger.

“Serafina offered me a getaway car.”

He laughed under his breath. “That sounds like her.”

“You’re not offended?”

“No.” He pushed her hair back from her face. “Your sister should know you have somewhere to go if you ever need it.”

“Even if it’s away from you?”

“Especially then.”

She looked up at him for a long moment. Then she bent and kissed his chest.

“Good husband.”

“Good wife.”

She made a small dissatisfied noise.

He thought about it. “My queen.”

“Better,” said Aurelia, and he pulled the blanket up over her shoulder. Just before she slept she heard him say it once more. Not as a title. Not a promise to obey. A thing he’d chosen to call her because he’d understood that loving her meant seeing the woman she’d always been. She had spent her whole life trying to become someone worth choosing, and she closed her eyes knowing she’d never once had to win him.

chapters.title: A Necklace on the Hit List
chapters.desc: She finishes the best necklace she’s ever made and lays it over her husband’s shoulders while he stares at his list. Then she makes him count the stones out loud.
chapters.epigraph: “Forty-one sapphires. Not one of them bought by Chen Si.”
chapters.content:
Three months after the wedding, on a hot Friday in the middle of August, at seventeen minutes past eleven, the necklace came up from the workshop in a black velvet case. Aurelia had been waiting for it for three years.

Not every minute of them. There had been other collections and other deadlines, a wedding, a husband whose work had a way of turning ordinary Tuesdays into emergencies. But the collar had never really left her head. Forty-one sapphires. The hardest thing she’d ever drawn.

Enzo put the case on the bench in front of her with the face of a man the entire jewellery trade had personally inconvenienced.

“Before you say anything, I want it known that this piece has aged me seven years.”

“You’re exaggerating.”

“Three, then.”

“Enzo.”

“Five. Final offer,” he said, and opened the lid.

She forgot to breathe. It lay on the black velvet like a strip of midnight. Forty-one stones, every one chosen for the depth of its blue and for how it answered the stones beside it, graduated along the curve towards the centre stone, which was larger and so dark it looked black until the light reached into it. The gold was very nearly invisible. From a little distance the sapphires seemed to hang in the air on their own. It wasn’t delicate, and it wasn’t loud. It was certain.

She reached for it and stopped a quarter-inch from the centre stone.

“Go on,” said Enzo. “I finished it, didn’t I?”

She lifted it. It had weight. She’d revised it, rejected a hundred and four stones, changed the settings twice, nearly abandoned the whole thing two winters running. And here it was, better than the version she’d held in her head.

“It’s beautiful,” she said.

“I know.” He squeezed her hand across the bench. “You counted those stones so many times I began to think you didn’t trust me.”

“I don’t trust anyone with forty-one sapphires.”

“Good. You shouldn’t. When will you sell it?”

“In the spring. At the big jewel sale overseas, with a proper catalogue. Every stone described. A private view first. Nobody gets it just because they have the money.” She closed the lid. “It’s going to say what this house can do.”

“You’ve become expensive,” said Enzo.

“I’ve always been expensive. People are only now noticing.”

He laughed, and kissed her forehead, and said her husband was a lucky man, and she said he was aware of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone rang a little after noon.

Mother.

Aurelia watched it ring twice. Then she answered.

“Hello, Mother.”

“Aurelia.” Vittoria’s voice was polished as ever, neither warm nor cold; the voice of a woman who’d long since decided that affection was best rationed. “I saw the photographs of your spring pieces. They were well received.”

“Thank you.”

A pause, and then, without any bridge at all: “Does your husband pay for the shop?”

Outside the glass a woman was bending to look at a pair of earrings. Lily was bringing out a tray.

“No.”

“Are you quite sure? A shop of that standard must be very costly, especially when you’re not yet established enough to—“

“Mother.”

Vittoria stopped.

“Did you ring to ask about my business,” said Aurelia, “or to find out whether a man’s paying for it?”

“It’s a reasonable question.”

“No. You’re asking whether I managed to build something without a man paying for it. My designs are mine. My people are paid from my accounts. My husband has never paid for my work.”

“Then he’s a very generous husband.”

“He is. With his time. With his attention. He lets me complain about stone dealers at dinner when he has a room of men waiting. He doesn’t pay for my work.”

“You’ve changed,” said Vittoria, after a silence.

“Yes.”

“I hope marriage hasn’t made you arrogant.”

Aurelia nearly laughed. “No. I think it’s made me less willing to explain myself.”

A small, disapproving sound. Then: “I should like to see the new collection some time.”

Not an apology. Not a word about the toast or the magazine. Only a request to be let into something Aurelia had made.

“You’re welcome to make an appointment.”

“An appointment?”

“It’s a shop, Mother. We keep a diary.”

Vittoria said nothing. Aurelia didn’t fill it. At last her mother said goodbye, and she said goodbye, and put the phone face down on the bench beside the collar. Forty-one sapphires. Not one of them bought by Chen Si. She found she was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the same hour, on the top floor of Chen Holdings, Chen Si was looking at nineteen names.

They stood in a neat column on a sheet of white paper. Nineteen men between the first trace of the old arrangement and the man who sat at the bottom of it.

Fu Jianguo.

“Explain,” he said.

Qian put a second folder beside the first. “The first six are in your father’s old books. The next five are in the money after his arrest. Four handled the assets when they were moved. The last four protected it, or were paid for protecting it.”

None of them were strangers. Some had built careers out of standing near his father. Two had spoken at the funeral. One of them had held Chen Si’s face in both hands at the graveside, when he was fifteen, and called him son.

“Which of them know we’re looking?”

“Three.” Qian named them.

Chen Si put a small mark beside each name. “Make the first of the three lose his port licence by Christmas. Nothing that comes back to us. Let the other two watch it happen.”

“And Fu?”

“Not yet. Quietly.”

“Of course.”

He’d imagined that name for years, in anger, in dreams, in the minute after waking when the past got there before he’d remembered what year it was. He’d imagined asking Fu why. The longer he dug, the clearer it became that Fu was only the man at the end of it. Each of the nineteen was a choice somebody had made: to lie, to look away, to decide that a dead man’s name was a fair price for a living man’s fortune. He’d thought revenge would feel like arriving somewhere. It looked like paperwork.

“Mrs. Chen is at the shop today,” said Qian. “She said Enzo was finishing a piece. She sounded pleased.”

Something eased round Chen Si’s eyes. Qian saw it.

“Tell the driver twenty minutes,” said Chen Si.

“Of course.” Qian paused at the door. “You’ve been married three months, Mr. Chen. It’s made you very nearly tolerable.”

Chen Si looked at him. Qian’s face was entirely neutral.

“Twenty minutes,” said Chen Si.

When he was alone again he picked up the black jade queen she’d left on his desk that morning, turned it once in his fingers, and set it down on the paper, beside the last name.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was standing in the middle of the shop when he came in, with the collar laid out on a velvet cushion, and her whole face lit when she saw him through the glass.

“Ah,” said Enzo. “The husband.”

Chen Si shook his hand. “Thank you for finishing it.”

“You haven’t even looked at it properly.”

“I’ve seen the photographs.”

“Photographs are not the same thing,” said Enzo, gathering his tools. “And don’t let her wear it in the kitchen. I won’t explain to an insurer why forty-one sapphires went into a soup.”

“That happened once,” said Aurelia.

“Once is enough,” said Enzo, and went.

She lifted the collar. “Look.”

He looked for a long time without saying anything. She watched his face. She’d wanted him to see this, the finished thing, not the sketches she’d shown him over dinner or the loose stones in their papers.

“It’s extraordinary,” he said.

“That’s all?”

“No. The stones look as though they chose each other. And the centre one’s different.”

“It’s the anchor.”

“Forty-one?”

“Forty-one.”

“May I?”

She understood him. She stepped close and laid it round his shoulders, over his white shirt, the stones lying just below his throat. It was absurdly beautiful on him. The blue went almost black against the white, and woke up only when he moved.

“Oh,” said Aurelia.

“What?”

“You look expensive.”

“I’ll take that as a compliment.”

“You should.”

She touched the centre stone straight with one finger, and her eyes fell on the folder he’d put down on the counter without thinking. The column of names. The black queen he’d carried with him, lying on the paper.

“Is that the list?”

“Yes.”

She didn’t touch it. She read it in silence, down to the last line.

“How many between you and him?”

“All nineteen.”

“Some of them are only men who looked away.”

“Some of them.”

“And you’ll find out which.”

“Yes.”

She picked up the queen, turned it over, and put it back down on the paper, squarely over the last name, so that the black jade covered it.

“Don’t forget what you’re doing it for. Your father. Your mother. The truth. Not so you can turn into something worse than what they did to you.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He took her hand. “I’m trying to.”

She nodded. She didn’t ask him to throw the list away; she knew better than to think a wound like his would close because somebody asked it to. She only wanted him to remember there was a life on the other side of the last name.

“Take it off,” she said, meaning the collar. “I’ve got a much better use for your attention. Come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The study at the top of the flat was half his and half hers now: his books next to her stone references, her sketches rolled in leather tubes, boxes of sample stones in their papers, the long desk where she worked late. Tonight the desk was bare except for a velvet cushion and the collar lying on it.

She shut the door.

“Sit.”

“An order?”

“Would you prefer a request?”

“Not particularly,” said Chen Si, and sat in the big chair.

“Hands on the arms.”

He put them there. She came and put the collar round his neck and fastened it behind him, and then stood at his back with her hands on his shoulders and leaned down to his ear.

“The first drawing had forty stones. Do you know why I changed it?”

“Because it needed another.”

“Very good. Tonight you’re going to count them. Slowly. Out loud. And you don’t get to do it without looking.”

“That seems unfair.”

“Life is difficult,” said Aurelia, and stood a mirror on the desk in front of him so he could see.

“One,” said Chen Si, and touched the first stone.

He went slowly, the way she’d told him to, along the curve. His fingertips never pressed a setting or let a nail touch the gold. “Seven.” “Eight.” She watched his hands in the glass. At the centre stone he stopped.

“Thirteen. It’s larger.”

“Same mine. Different proportions.”

“Fourteen.”

The counting became a rhythm between them. Every number an acknowledgement. Every stone one she’d chosen and inspected and rejected and finally let in. By twenty-one she’d come round to his side and slipped her fingers under the edge of his collar where it lay against his skin.

“Twenty-two.”

“Mm.”

“Are you distracted?”

“Yes.”

“Then concentrate.”

“I’m trying.”

“Try harder.”

“Thirty-one. How many did you throw out?”

“A hundred and four. Too pale, too dark, a feather in the wrong place. Some beautiful alone that didn’t belong with the others.”

“And you found forty-one.”

“Thirty-two,” she prompted, and kissed his temple.

“Thirty-three. You’re interfering.”

“I’m supervising.”

“I’d prefer you stopped distracting me.”

So she stopped. She went and stood by the desk with her hands folded and looked at him with an expression far too innocent to be trusted, and he stared at her in the mirror and then laughed, the real one, low and helpless.

“Thirty-five,” he said, when he could. “Thirty-nine. Forty.” His fingers came to the last small stone by the clasp. Not the biggest or the brightest. The one that finished the line. “Forty-one.”

“Correct.”

“Is there a prize?”

“You’re wearing the prize.”

“That isn’t mine. You made it.”

She stepped in between his knees. “Then what do you want?”

“You,” said Chen Si. Not a demand. Just true.

“You have me.”

He reached for her waist, and she put a hand flat on his chest. “Wait.” He stopped. “Do you know what I was thinking when I drew it? About the woman who’d wear it.
