I wanted her to be able to walk into any room without asking anyone’s leave to be there. I wanted the necklace to look as though it had finally found somebody worthy of it.”

“That’s what you made.”

“And it’s going to auction, and somebody will buy it, and that’s the point.”

“I’d buy it.”

“You can’t. It would be ridiculous.”

“I’ve been ridiculous before.”

“Not with my business,” said Aurelia, and kissed him, and this time when his hand came to her back she let it stay. The sapphires moved against his shirt, and her fingers went into his hair, and she climbed into his lap in the big chair with the collar still round his neck and the mirror on the desk showing the two of them to nobody. He kept his other hand on the arm of the chair, because nobody had told him to move it, until she took it and put it where she wanted it.

Afterwards he asked her why she’d brought the collar home.

“Your list has nineteen names,” she said, with her cheek on his shoulder. “This has forty-one stones. I know it isn’t the same. I wanted you to have something in front of you tonight that wasn’t Fu.”

He covered her hand on the centre stone with his.

“I see it,” he said. “And I see you. My queen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two that morning she was alone in the study with the collar on the cushion in front of her, unable to sleep, hearing her mother’s voice ask whether her husband paid for the shop. She took the catalogue sheet the auction house had sent and uncapped her red pen, and where it said Lot, title to be confirmed, she wrote two words, and underlined them twice.

Numero Uno.

Then she went back to bed, and lay down against her husband’s back, and slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city the next afternoon, on the top floor, the black queen still lay over the last name on the list. Beside the paper now was a photograph Qian had printed, at her request, from the shop’s own camera: Aurelia standing behind her husband, settling a collar of sapphires round his shoulders. In it Chen Si was smiling. Not the controlled thing he wore in meetings. Not the thin smile that made men reconsider what they’d been about to say.

He looked at it for a long time. Nineteen names. One black queen. Forty-one stones. For the first time in years the future had something in it besides the last name on a page. It had a woman putting the best thing she’d ever made under the lights of an auction room in the spring, and he intended to be in the front row when the bidding began.

chapters.title: Chen Si Lost an Argument (Once)
chapters.desc: A grey car follows her, and he wants two men behind her everywhere. She wins the argument with a cancelled shipment, three days at Zhao’s range and a page of red ink.
chapters.epigraph: “Frightened men get controlling. It doesn’t make them right.”
chapters.content:
The second shop opened on a Wednesday in September, because Aurelia liked Wednesdays. Lily had spent three weeks arguing for a Saturday, for the foot traffic.

“Saturday’s too obvious,” said Aurelia.

“You’re impossible.”

“So I’m told.”

It stood two hundred metres along Harbour Road from the first, on the ground floor of an old stone building with tall windows and a narrow brass sign. Larger than the first, and she’d refused to make it grander for the sake of it: no dripping chandeliers, no acres of marble. Pale limestone, dark walnut, brushed brass, the light placed so the stones did the talking. At the back, behind a glass wall, two bench jewellers were already at work, so that anyone who came in could see the pieces didn’t simply appear in velvet boxes. They were made. By people. With hands.

At ten she stood under the sign in a cream suit with Enzo beside her.

“You’ve done it,” he said.

“We’ve done it.”

“Don’t include me. I only complained for three years.”

“Four.”

“Then I deserve more credit.”

Across the road, in the back of his car, Chen Si watched her laugh for the photographer.

Chen Si: The sign looks good.

Aurelia: You haven’t even come in.

Chen Si: I can see it.

Aurelia: You are not allowed to review my architecture from a car. Come inside, husband.

He went inside.

By noon the shop was full: buyers, collectors, two journalists, and a number of people more interested in the business behind her name than in the jewellery. She moved through them as if she’d been born doing it. She remembered names, asked after daughters, explained the difference between two sapphires without making anyone feel stupid for asking, and quietly booked a private appointment for a woman who wanted something for her daughter’s wedding. He’d watched her take rooms apart before. This was different. This was a room she’d made.

A journalist held out the morning’s business pages. THE QUEEN OF HARBOUR ROAD: AURELIA CHEN OPENS A SECOND HOUSE.

“Do you like it?”

“I like the part about the second shop.”

“Not the queen?”

“I’ve never needed a crown to run a business,” said Aurelia.

By the window Chen Si heard it, and smiled, and folded his copy of the paper into his inside pocket to keep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The grey saloon appeared at eighteen minutes past six.

It had been behind her car for three turns before she noticed it. Harbour Road was slow at that hour. Cars sat behind one another longer than they should. But when her driver changed lanes it changed lanes, and when they turned towards the river it turned.

“Take the next left,” she said. It took the next left. “Don’t go home. Go on towards the hotel. The long way.”

She rang Chen Si.

“Where are you?”

“Near the river. There’s a grey saloon behind us. Four turns, perhaps five.”

A silence, not long. Long enough.

“Don’t look at it again. Stay in the car. I’m sending people.”

“Don’t come yourself.”

“Aurelia.”

“I’m telling you not to come alone.”

She heard his chair go back and a door open. “Keep me on the line.”

Six minutes later two black cars came up out of nowhere behind the saloon. One got in front of it and one came alongside, and it slowed and stopped, and her driver went on along the river without it.

“He’s been stopped,” said Chen Si.

“What are you going to do?”

His silence told her.

“Don’t,” she said. “Not before you know who he is.”

A pause. “I’ll wait until I know.”

It wasn’t a promise to do nothing. It was enough to keep her from arguing while she was still in the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man turned out to be a private investigator, hired through a go-between to photograph her and log where she went. Who had paid the go-between, nobody yet knew. There was no sign he’d meant to come near her. That didn’t help.

Chen Si met him two nights later in a garage on the edge of the city, under a strip light, with the grey saloon parked beside him.

“Who hired you?”

“I was paid to follow a woman. I was given a photograph and an address. That’s all.”

“Do you know what happens to men who follow my wife?”

The man swallowed. “I didn’t know she was your wife.”

“That isn’t an answer.” Chen Si turned away. “Qian. Find out.”

The man reached out and caught his sleeve.

It was a mistake. The garage went very quiet. Chen Si turned back, took the man’s wrist, and put him into the side of the car hard enough that the panel rang. He held him there and spoke low, almost gently.

“Don’t touch me.”

He let go. The man slid down the door holding his wrist and began, very fast, to offer names. Chen Si was already walking out.

“His licence,” said Qian at the door.

“Have it pulled.”

“And the car?”

“Crush it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time he got home she’d heard about the car.

She was in the kitchen in a pink apron that said KISS THE COOK in white letters across the front, stirring something with a wooden spoon. He stopped in the doorway.

“Interesting.”

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.” She turned off the flame. “You had the car crushed. And his wrist.”

“He was following you. He knew where you went. He knew your hours.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t ask me to treat it as nothing,” he said, sharper than he meant.

“I’m not. I’m asking you to understand that frightening a man isn’t the same as finding out who sent him.” She came closer. “You’re allowed to be worried. You’re allowed to be angry. You don’t get to turn every fear into an order. And you don’t get to decide that the only way to keep me safe is to make my world smaller.”

He touched her cheek. “I don’t want your world smaller.”

“Then stop trying to put two men in it.”

“One?”

“No.”

“Half of one?”

She laughed in spite of herself, and he kissed her. It wasn’t apologetic. It was full of everything neither of them had found a way to say, and he walked her back against the counter with his hand at her waist and her fist in his shirt.

“You’re distracting me.”

“You’re wearing an apron that says kiss the cook. I took it as an instruction.”

“Something’s burning,” she said, and pushed him off, and he laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The argument lasted eleven days.

On the fourth he sent a security proposal to her office: two men, at all times, one close and one at a distance. She sent it back with red ink on every page. On the fifth he offered one. She sent it back with a single word. On the sixth Qian suggested, very carefully, that perhaps a driver with advanced training might be a compromise, and she told him that if he went on acting as her husband’s representative in a marital dispute she would start invoicing him. Qian stopped suggesting things. On the seventh she noticed a man in the café across from the new shop who’d been nursing the same coffee for four hours, and rang her husband.

“Remove him.”

“He isn’t inside.”

“Would you like me to come over there and remove him myself?”

A pause. “He’s leaving.”

On the tenth day a parcel of loose stones meant for the new shop’s first private view was held at the port. Somebody had altered the paperwork. The broker wanted a fresh declaration. If it took a week, she’d lose the appointment and a dealer she’d spent two years earning.

She rang Chen Si.

“I’ll have it handled,” he said.

“No. If you send your people, the broker will be too frightened to sign anything and the stones will sit there a month. I need the paperwork corrected, not a man made to sweat.” She looked at the calendar on her desk. “I have a solution. But you have to agree to something.”

“Go on.”

“Three days at Zhao’s range. Properly. Not ten minutes with someone telling me where to stand. Three days.”

“Why Zhao?”

“Because I trust him.”

“You want to learn to shoot because a man followed you?”

“I want to learn because I don’t like being told my safety depends entirely on somebody else being in the room.”

A long silence. “And in return?”

“One man. Outside, never in the shop, never in a private appointment unless I ask, and only until you find out who paid for the grey car. My driver stays. Qian has my route when I’m off my usual hours. And you stop tracking my phone.”

The silence this time was a different kind.

“Chen Si?”

“We’ll discuss it.”

“We’ll discuss it now.”

“All right,” he said at last, very quietly.

“Good. I’ll send you the terms in writing.”

“You’ve already written them.”

“Of course I have,” said Aurelia. “You’re going to lose this argument.”

“We’ll see.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao’s range was under an old warehouse outside the city, on no map anybody could buy, through a door that looked like a storage unit’s. She came on the Monday in black trousers and flat shoes, and he was already there, alone.

“You’re early.”

“I was told to be.”

“Good. Put your bag down.”

He began with rules, not the gun. Where to stand. How to listen. What not to touch, ever. What to do when she wasn’t sure, and how to tell when she was getting tired. When she got something wrong he corrected it, and when she asked he answered, and when she tried to get ahead of him he stopped her.

“You’re impatient.”

“So my husband tells me.”

“He’s right. Again.”

By the second day she’d stopped trying to guess his corrections before he made them and her hands had gone steady.

“You learn fast,” he said. “Don’t be pleased. It makes you sloppy.”

“Do you ever compliment anyone?”

“Rarely. They get annoying.”

On the second afternoon he gave her a bottle of water and leaned on the wall while she sat on the bench.

“How long have you known him?”

“Since I was fifteen.”

“Was he always like this? Convinced the whole world’s his responsibility?”

Zhao thought about it. “He smiled more, before.”

“Before his father?”

“Before a lot of things.” He drank. “You know about his mother?”

“Some.”

“She was ill a long time. She didn’t tell him how bad it was, because he was away in the north getting close to Fu’s people, and she didn’t want him to come back. He was gone three weeks. When he got home she’d been dead four days.” He looked at the far wall. “He’s never forgiven himself for not knowing.”

Aurelia’s fingers tightened on the bottle.

“He’s never told me that.”

“He might not. He thinks if he tells you, he’s making you carry it.”

“That isn’t how marriage works.”

Zhao’s mouth moved, not quite a smile. “Try telling him.” He pushed off the wall. “Don’t tell him I told you.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“Only when I’m caught.”

On the third day he made her do everything twice as carefully, because she’d begun to feel comfortable and that, he said, was when people got hurt. At the end he checked every piece of equipment himself and put it away.

“Better,” he said.

“That’s almost a compliment.”

“He’ll still worry. He’ll probably ask for two men again.”

“I know.”

“Don’t mistake learning for being bulletproof. And don’t let him make you feel guilty for wanting to look after yourself.” He picked up his jacket. “Frightened men get controlling. It doesn’t make them right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was waiting by the door of the flat when Zhao dropped her off, with his hands in his pockets and her phone in one of them. She’d left it on the kitchen counter that morning.

She looked at it in his hand, and then at him. And she knew. She’d known since his silence on the telephone.

“How long have you been tracking my phone?”

He went still. It was very slight. She saw it.

“Since the wedding.”

“Since May?”

“Yes.”

She took the phone out of his hand and opened the settings, and there it was, a permanent line from her location to his.

“Four months. Without telling me.”

“I wanted to know you were safe.”

“You could have asked.”

“I knew you’d say no.”

“Then you knew I hadn’t agreed.” She put the phone down on the hall table. “You can’t build a marriage on the idea that if you think a thing’s necessary, you don’t need my permission.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

She expected one of the usual answers. Because I was worried. Because I could.

“Because I was afraid,” said Chen Si.

“Of what?”

“Of not knowing.” He looked down at his hands. “When my mother died I wasn’t there. She’d been dead four days before I found out. I keep thinking, if I’d known sooner. If I’d rung. If I’d come home a week earlier.” He stopped. “I know it doesn’t make sense. Not knowing where you are brings it back.”

The anger in her chest didn’t go anywhere. It just became more complicated.

“I’m not your mother,” she said.

“I know.”

“And I won’t punish you for being frightened. But you can’t make me pay for what happened to her.”

“I know.”

“Then we need a different arrangement. First, turn it off.”

He took out his phone and did it, there in the hall, without a moment’s hesitation.

“Second. I want yours.”

“Mine?”

“Your location. The same as you had of mine. Then we both have it, and we both know, and either of us can turn it off by saying so. No hidden devices. No asking Qian where the other one is because we’re too proud to ask ourselves.”

“That last one seems very specific.”

“It is.”

He shared it. She watched the confirmation appear on her screen.

“One man,” she said. “Outside. A second only if there’s a real threat, and then we talk about it, together.”

“Agreed. And if you ever feel unsafe, you ring me.”

“That isn’t a rule. That’s common sense.”

“Then we agree.” He touched her cheek. “I’m sorry. I won’t do it again.”

He bent his head, and she put a finger on his lips.

“Eleven days,” she said. “You argued with me for eleven days.”

“I made reasonable proposals.”

“You made the same proposal eleven different ways. And you lost.”

He considered disputing it. She watched him consider it.

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “I lost.”

“Say it again.”

“I lost the argument.”

“Beautiful,” said Aurelia, and took him by the collar and kissed him, and he let her, and he didn’t argue about that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday the dishwasher died with a noise like a dying engine and a pool of grey water. Maintenance could come on Monday. She rang Zhao.

He arrived forty minutes later with a toolbox. Chen Si came out of the study and looked at the toolbox and then at his wife.

“You called Zhao to fix the dishwasher.”

“You’re busy.”

“I can fix a dishwasher.”

She tilted her head. “Can you?”

He opened his mouth and shut it again.

Zhao lay on the kitchen floor with his head in the machine for some time. Then he sat up holding something between finger and thumb. A tiny round sapphire, deep blue, loose from its setting.

“Do you usually wash your gemstones?” he said.

“I lost that in March.”

Chen Si looked at it. “How did it get in the—“

“Don’t.”

And Zhao began to laugh. Not his short dry sound. He sat on the kitchen floor of the most feared man in the city and laughed until he had to wipe his eyes.

“I’ve spent nine years watching him make grown men afraid to speak,” he said, “and now he’s standing in his own kitchen asking his wife how a sapphire got into the dishwasher.”

Aurelia had to put the stone down. Chen Si looked at the two of them, both helpless, and after a while, despite himself, he smiled.

Zhao wouldn’t take money for it, so she made him lunch. Fish and greens and the soup she’d been trying to get right for a month. Halfway through she put the little sapphire down beside her husband’s plate.

“Forty-one in Numero Uno,” he said. “One in the dishwasher.”

“Don’t make it sound as though I’ve lost my mind.”

“How many sapphires do you have in this house?” said Zhao.

Aurelia thought about it. “Not enough.”

“You two deserve each other,” said Zhao, into his bowl.

Under the table she found her husband’s hand. He’d lost an argument. He’d given up a secret he should never have kept. And somewhere between the range and a broken dishwasher, he’d begun to understand that keeping his wife safe didn’t mean keeping her inside the reach of his arm every minute of the day.

chapters.title: The Song Family Is Coming to Dinner
chapters.desc: Her mother writes to invite herself to dinner. Chen Si cooks the fish, Aurelia leaves the dishwasher whining on purpose, and at the door her mother names the one man he can’t stand.
chapters.epigraph: “Leave one flaw.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on the first Wednesday of October. Not a telephone call, not a message passed through Serafina, not one of the short, careful texts her mother sent when she wanted something. A letter, on paper thick enough to mean something, in Vittoria’s own hand, delivered to the shop by a man who left no name.

Dear Aurelia,

Your father and I should like to have dinner with you and Chen Si. It has been some time since we sat down together properly, and I think it is time we made an effort.

We have heard about the second house. It is a considerable achievement.

We would like to be proud of you.

Saturday the twelfth would suit us. Please let us know whether you can receive us at home.

Mother

Aurelia read it three times and put it down on the desk. We would like to be proud of you. Not we are. Not we should have been there. An offer, phrased as if her mother’s pride were still something she might earn if she behaved.

She picked up her pen and wrote under it: Saturday the twelfth, at seven, at ours. And sent it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si found it that evening on the dining table beside a catalogue and was still holding it when she came down.

“You’ve read it.”

“You left it on the table.”

“An excellent defence.”

“Your parents are coming to dinner. The night before your father’s birthday.”

“Are you going to ask me whether I want them here?”

“Do you?”

She opened the fridge. “I don’t know.”

“Then we can cancel.”

“No.”

“All right.”

She turned round and studied him. “You’re not going to tell me it’s a bad idea?”

“You didn’t ask me whether I thought it was a good one.”

“You’re learning.”

“I’ve had an excellent teacher. May I ask one thing? Why now?”

“Perhaps she misses me.”

He watched her. “I could say your mother has never been very good at missing people without wanting something from them.”

“That isn’t clever. It’s rude.”

“It’s also possible.”

“Don’t make it difficult before it’s happened,” said Aurelia. “And don’t turn it into a business meeting.”

“I want to meet the people who raised my wife.”

“That’s a dangerous sentence. One of them’s going to disappoint you.”

“Then I’ll make sure the dinner’s good,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t intend to stop the dinner. But the timing bothered him, and on the Thursday he asked Qian a question, and Qian, who had been collecting small observations all summer and not yet put them in a row, put them in a row.

“She began asking about you in June,” said Qian. “Two old business associates. A retired banker. And a lawyer who worked on your father’s defence before the arrest.”

Chen Si looked up.

“She asked whether the official account was complete. And about you and Fu Jianguo.”

“How much did she get?”

“Not much. She was persistent.”

“She spent the summer investigating me.”

“She may have wanted to understand the man her daughter married.” Qian met his look. “Or she may have been looking for something to use. There’s a scheme going round the Song Group’s friends. A redevelopment at the approach to the new harbour bridge. The details are thin.”

“Find out who’s behind it. Don’t go near Mrs. Song.”

At the door Qian paused. “Will you tell Mrs. Chen?”

Chen Si looked at the letter on his desk. He didn’t like secrets in a marriage. He liked even less the idea of her being pulled into something without knowing it. But if he told her before he had anything solid, her mother’s invitation would become one more problem he’d already decided how to solve, and that was precisely the thing she’d asked him never to do.

“Not yet,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday afternoon he came into the kitchen and found her bent over a glass vase of pale pink garden roses on the island, trying to pull a torn petal off one of them. The stem shifted under her hand and a thorn went into the side of her finger.

“Ah.”

He had her hand before she’d finished the syllable. “Let me see.”

“It’s a thorn.”

“Sit.”

She gave him a look. He gave her one back. She sat. He fetched the little first-aid tin from the drawer and knelt in front of her stool and took the splinter of thorn out with tweezers, frowning at it as if it were an engraving, his eyebrows drawn together.

“You’re treating it like surgery.”

“I’m trying not to make it worse.”

She looked at the top of his head and something in her chest hurt.

“Do you think they’re ugly?” she said. “The roses?”

He glanced at them. One torn petal. One flower a little crooked. The stems not quite even. “No.”

“They’re not perfect.”

“Neither am I.”

“That’s not the point.” She looked at her finger. “I keep thinking about what she’ll notice. Whether the flat’s too formal. Whether the food’s right. Whether she’ll look round and decide I haven’t done enough. I don’t even know why I care.”

“Because you still want her to be pleased,” said Chen Si. “That isn’t weakness.”

Her eyes filled, which was absurd, and she turned her face away. It wasn’t the roses. It was the letter. It was one sentence in her mother’s hand. She’d opened two shops and built a house from nothing and married a man she loved without letting either family write a word of the terms, and still one line of Vittoria’s could make her sixteen again.

He put the tweezers down. “Come here.”

She cried into his shirt, briefly, furiously, ashamed of it.

“I’m crying over a rose.”

“Then let the rose be the reason.” He wiped her face with his thumb. “Leave one flaw.”

“What?”

“In the flowers. In the dinner. In the house. Leave one thing imperfect. Your mother’s coming to dinner. Not a panel of judges.”

She laughed through it. “That’s easy for you. You haven’t got a mother coming to dinner.”

It was out before she could stop it.

She saw it land. Not anger. Something quieter: the face of a man walking past a room in his own house that had been locked for years.

“Chen Si—“

“It’s all right.”

“No. I didn’t mean—“

“I know what you meant.” He touched her cheek. “Leave one flaw, Aurelia.”

She took his hand and kissed the palm, and held it there for a while, and said she was sorry, twice, and he shook his head both times. Then she put the vase back in the middle of the island with the torn petal still on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By four it was raining and he was cooking, sleeves up, a whole fish on the board, ginger and spring onion, a clear broth, mushrooms in a little dish.

“Are you planning to feed her or challenge her?”

“Both, if necessary.”

She reached for a spring onion and he caught her wrist. “You’re wearing silk. Set the table.”

“That isn’t cooking.”

“It’s very important work. Please.”

She set four places and moved the roses half an inch and left the torn petal where it was. When she came back she ran the dishwasher, which was full, and halfway through its cycle it began to make a small high whine, the noise it had made ever since Zhao had lain on the floor with his head inside it.

Chen Si looked round. “Is that broken again?”

“No.”

They looked at each other. Then he understood.

“You’re leaving it.”

“Yes.”

“During dinner. With your parents.”

“It isn’t broken. It’s slightly annoying.”

“It’s an irritating noise.”

“It’s an imperfect noise,” said Aurelia, and he laughed out loud over the fish, and she kissed his cheek and called him a good husband.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came at seven. Song Weiren first, in a dark suit, with a bottle of wine and the uneasy courtesy of a man greeting a son-in-law who’d become a great deal more powerful than anyone in his own house.

“Mr. Chen.”

“Mr. Song.”

Then Vittoria, in pale grey, wearing a necklace Aurelia knew from her mother’s own mother’s box. They kissed the air beside each other’s cheeks.

“Your home is lovely,” said Vittoria. “Very tasteful.”

Her eyes passed over the roses on the way to the dining room and stopped, for a fraction of a second, on the torn petal. Aurelia saw her see it. Neither of them said a word. In the kitchen the dishwasher whined.

“Is something wrong?”

“Only the dishwasher.”

“Shouldn’t you turn it off?”

“It’s fine,” said Aurelia, and held her mother’s eyes, and then asked whether she’d like a drink.

Dinner began politely. Her father asked Chen Si about his businesses and Chen Si answered without giving away anything he didn’t want to. Her mother asked about the new shop, its clients, the next collection, and Aurelia answered every question without making anything larger or smaller than it was.

“Does Chen Si help you with the business?”

“Not with money.”

“I wasn’t asking that.”

“Then what were you asking?”

“Whether he advises you.”

“Only when she asks,” said Chen Si, putting a dish down in front of his wife.

He’d made the fish perfectly. The skin lifted clean away, the flesh came apart in petals. He served Vittoria first and said, “Please, while it’s warm,” and served Song Weiren the cheek because he’d noticed him look at it. He filled water glasses before anyone asked. He listened without interrupting. He wasn’t trying to impress anyone, which was what made him so hard to fault.

At some point, reaching past her to move a dish nearer her mother, he let his hand come to rest at the back of Aurelia’s neck. Without thinking. His thumb just under her hair, warm, perfectly still.

Her shoulders went tight.

He felt it at once. He didn’t take his hand away suddenly, and he didn’t ask her anything in front of her parents. He only softened it, and left it there, and let her choose.

Because it had come back anyway. A show, when she was sixteen. Hot lights, a dress she’d worked on for weeks, and her mother standing behind her with her fingers digging into exactly that place, pressing her shoulders down and her chin up. Smile. Don’t embarrass me. And when she didn’t move fast enough, harder. She’d smiled. She’d learned to keep her face perfectly still while somebody else’s fingers hurt.

There was no pressure in this hand. No instruction in it at all.

Under the table she found his wrist and touched it, and his fingers loosened, and he looked at her. She gave him the smallest smile. He gave it back, and took his hand away, and went on serving fish.

Vittoria had seen. “You’re very attentive to her.”

“She’s my wife,” said Chen Si.

The dishwasher whined. Aurelia smiled into her rice.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was over the tea that Vittoria said, “Your family’s been in business a long time, haven’t they?”

“Yes.”

“Your father was very respected.”

“Some people thought so.”

“That must have been hard. Losing him so young.”

“It was.”

“Do you still keep up with any of his old associates?”

“Some.”

“And Fu Jianguo?”

Nobody dropped a glass. Nobody moved. But the air in the room tightened, and Aurelia felt it go, like a wire being drawn.

Chen Si put his cup down. “Why do you ask?”

“He and your father were close, weren’t they? Such a shame how it ended.”

“Vittoria,” said Song Weiren. “Perhaps we leave business aside.”

“Of course.” She turned to her daughter. “The fish is very good.”

“Chen Si made it,” said Aurelia, looking at her mother, and knew her husband had recognised that question for exactly what it was. Not curiosity. A door being tried.

Her father asked about the shops again later, with real interest this time, how many people she employed and whether she meant to open a third.

“Not yet. I want both to run properly first.”

“That’s sensible.” He looked into his tea, and then said, without looking up, “You’ve built something substantial.”

It was the first time in her life he’d spoken about her work without measuring it against somebody else’s.

“Thank you, Ba,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to ten, in the hall, with her coat on, Vittoria said, “Might I have a word with you, Chen Si?”

He looked at Aurelia. She nodded and went three steps into the corridor, no further.

“The bridge,” said Vittoria, low. “The family has an interest in the redevelopment at the approach. Approval has become complicated. We need someone to speak to Fu Jianguo. You have enough standing with him at least to arrange a meeting.”

“Why would I speak to Fu?”

“Because it matters. To the family. She needn’t be involved.”

His voice went cool. “Then you shouldn’t have asked me in her home.”

“Surely personal history can be put aside for—“

“Not this history.”

“Your father and he were friends. Surely you won’t let an old grievance stand in the way of—“

“Mother,” said Aurelia, and came back up the hall.

Vittoria turned. “This doesn’t concern you.”

Aurelia laughed, one short incredulous breath. “You came into my home and asked my husband to go and beg favours of the man who put his father in the cell he died in, and it doesn’t concern me?”

Song Weiren looked at his wife sharply.

“That isn’t what I said.”

“It’s what you asked. You spent the whole summer finding out about him. You knew exactly who Fu Jianguo was.”

For the first time all evening Vittoria had nothing ready.

“I was trying to understand,” she said at last.

“Then you should have asked me.”

“I didn’t want to upset you.”

“Then you should have thought about that before you asked him to do something you knew would hurt him.”

“Vittoria,” said Song Weiren. “We’re going.”

At the door Vittoria looked back at Chen Si. “Think about it.”

“I have,” he said, and held the door. “Goodnight, Mrs. Song.”

Her father stopped on the step. “Thank you for dinner, Aurelia.”

“Goodnight, Ba.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When the door had shut, she turned on him. “How long have you known? About the summer?”

“Since Thursday. I wanted to be sure what she was looking for before I told you.”

“And?”

“Not entirely.”

“She wanted you to petition Fu. For a bridge. She knows you hate him.”

“She knows I have history with him.”

“She knows, Chen Si.”

He was silent for a moment. “Perhaps.”

She walked three steps towards the dining room and came back. “I hate that she looked at you across our table and talked about your father as if he were a scheduling problem.”

“I didn’t want her to spoil the evening.”

“She didn’t,” said Aurelia. Behind them the four places were still laid, the roses still in the middle with their one torn petal, and in the kitchen the dishwasher was still whining away to itself. She laughed. “The dishwasher survived.”

“Barely.”

“Come here.”

She took his shirt and kissed him against the door, hard. He let her, one hand at her waist and the other at her face, but when she tried to push it further he slowed her. Not by stepping back. By gentling her, his mouth going soft against hers and his thumb moving on her cheek, until she stopped trying to make the kiss into an answer to everything that had just happened.

“What’s that for?” he said, with his forehead against hers.

“For coming home with me.”

“I live here.”

“I know.” She touched his jaw. “You don’t have to let me defend you from my mother, you know.”

“Is that what you were doing?”

“I was defending our home,” said Aurelia. “And you. Mostly you.”

He pulled her in and held her against his chest. After a while she lifted her head.

“Did you turn the dishwasher off?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“You’re leaving it running all night?”

“Perhaps.”

“You’re a menace.”

“And you married me,” she said. “Any regrets?”

He pushed a strand of hair back behind her ear and looked at her for a long time. “Not one.”

Behind them the dishwasher whined, and neither of them went to turn it off.

chapters.title: What Her Father Wants
chapters.desc: Over risotto at Da Gianni, her father asks Chen Si to write to Fu Jianguo. Then he admits he’s already told Fu no.
chapters.epigraph: “I just didn’t want you to think nobody in that house saw.”
chapters.content:
Da Gianni hadn’t changed in twenty years: the same dark tables, the same black-and-white photographs of old Milanese streets, the same waiter, who remembered that Chen Si drank sparkling water and that Aurelia always ordered the risotto before she’d properly read the menu. She’d chosen the restaurant. Her father had chosen the lunch, on the Thursday after the dinner. She hadn’t missed the distinction.

“You’re early,” said Song Weiren.

She kissed his cheek. “You invited us.”

“I thought you might be busy.”

“I am. I made time.”

For the first few minutes it was ordinary. He asked about the new shop, and she said the workshop was running well but she wanted another senior bench jeweller before the year was out.

“That sounds expensive.”

“Good work usually is.”

He smiled a little. Across the table Chen Si watched her over his glass. He liked how she talked about the business. She never made it sound like a favour somebody had done her. She talked about it as a thing she’d built and meant to keep.

Song Weiren waited until the first course was down.

“I wanted to talk to you, Chen Si. About Fu Jianguo.”

Aurelia’s fork stopped.

“I thought it better to say it straight out. Fu’s been making things difficult on the bridge. He has a hand on certain approvals, and the people involved won’t move without his blessing. You have connections. I’m asking for a letter. An introduction. Something that would make him willing to sit down.”

“Ba,” said Aurelia. “We talked about this on Saturday.”

“We talked about your mother’s request. This is me asking him, directly.”

Chen Si’s eyes didn’t leave her father’s face. “You want me to write to the man who destroyed my father.”

Song Weiren looked honestly blank. “Your father and Fu were partners. Close associates.”

“Fu arranged the evidence that put my father in a cell. He paid men to contradict him. He made sure the truth never got near anyone who could have helped. My father died in custody. My mother waited for him to come home until she died as well.”

A glass chimed somewhere behind Aurelia. Somebody laughed by the window. At their table nobody moved.

“I didn’t know,” said Song Weiren.

“You didn’t ask.”

Her father took that in. Aurelia had known he wasn’t close to Chen Si, and that he’d never understood the whole of it. She hadn’t known how little he understood.

“Why did you want him to write it?” she said.

“The project matters.”

“Enough to send him to the man who ruined his family?”

“I knew there’d been a disagreement.”

“A disagreement,” said Chen Si.

Her father looked down at the tablecloth. “I chose the wrong word. I’m sorry.”

For a moment she thought Chen Si would stand up and end it. Instead he picked up his glass and drank, and put it down.

“Thank you,” he said. It wasn’t forgiveness. It was acknowledgement.

✦ ✦ ✦

The risotto came. Her father barely touched his.

“There’s something else,” he said at last. “Fu came to see me in September, before I thought of asking you. He wanted fifteen per cent of the bridge, in return for seeing the approvals through. For his son. Fu Kang. He’d hold it. A family arrangement, Fu said. For the next generation.”

“And you refused,” said Chen Si.

“I didn’t build that company to hand fifteen per cent of it to a man who’s never done a day’s work for it. I told him if his son wanted a share he could bring something of value. He didn’t care for that.”

There was no pride in it. He wasn’t trying to sound like a hero. It was just what he’d done.

“Then why ask me to write?”

Song Weiren looked uncomfortable. “Because now the whole thing’s in danger. I thought you might make him reconsider.”

“By giving him access to me.” Chen Si leaned back. “Fu doesn’t want a conversation, Mr. Song. He wants leverage. He came to you for fifteen per cent, and when you said no he waited for you to come to me.”

Aurelia saw the same thing arrive in her husband’s face that had just arrived in her own head. Fu had used her father as a door. A letter from Chen Si, a meeting, the two of them in one room, and the whole old history made into something useful to the man who’d started it.

“You should have told us about the fifteen per cent,” she said.

“You’re right.”

“Not because we’d necessarily have helped. Because you should have been honest about what was going on.”

“I understand.”

“Then why lunch?”

He hesitated. “Because I wanted to see you.”

“That isn’t very convincing.”

“No,” said her father, and accepted that too.

She’d stopped eating. Chen Si looked at her plate.

“You haven’t finished.”

“I’m thinking.”

“That usually makes you hungry.” He pushed his plate an inch towards her. “Try this.”

She shook her head, and instead took the last spoonful of her own and held it out to him across the table.

“I can order you more,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I want to.”

He leaned forward and took it, his eyes on hers.

“Good?”

“Very.”

“You’re biased.”

“Completely.”

Across the table Song Weiren watched them. It wasn’t the gesture. It was how easy it was. She didn’t ask permission to feed her husband, and he didn’t make anything of letting her. They simply knew each other. He’d spent years thinking a daughter should be guided and corrected and readied for the world. He hadn’t understood how much of that guiding had turned into weight. Now here she sat, giving her last bite to a man who’d never once asked her to be smaller, and he couldn’t remember when he’d stopped knowing how to speak to her.

Chen Si’s phone buzzed against the table. He looked at it and stood. “Excuse me. Two minutes.”

When he’d gone out to the street her father sat looking at the door for a while.

“He doesn’t raise his voice,” he said.

“No.”

“I thought he’d raise it. When I said disagreement. I’d have raised mine.”

“He doesn’t need to,” said Aurelia. “People usually wish he would.”

Song Weiren nodded slowly, as if that confirmed something he’d been told at a dinner and not believed. Then he turned his cup round on its saucer, once, twice.

“Your mother called me a fool,” he said. “When I told Fu no. In front of the staff. She said I’d thrown the bridge away for my pride, and that a man who couldn’t swallow fifteen per cent to keep a project alive had no business running a company.”

Aurelia went very still.

“I’m not telling you so you’ll take my side,” said her father. “I’m telling you because I think she wrote to you afterwards. Didn’t she. To come to dinner.”

“Yes.”

“We would like to be proud of you,” said Song Weiren, and she stared at him, and he gave her a small, tired smile. “She read it to me before she sent it. I said it was a cruel line. She said it was an honest one.”

“Which is it?”

He thought about it, honestly, the way Chen Si thought about things.

“Both,” he said. “She’s never been able to tell the difference. I used to think that was strength.” He looked down at his cold risotto. “When you were nine you came second in a piano examination in Milan. Do you remember? She didn’t speak to you on the train home. Two hours. I sat opposite and read the paper. I’ve thought about that train more this year than in the fifteen years since.”

“Why this year?”

“Because I watched you walk out of my birthday onto that balcony,” said her father, “and I looked at my cigar.”

She didn’t say anything. She couldn’t. Through the window she could see Chen Si on the pavement with his back to the glass and his phone to his ear, standing perfectly still while some unfortunate man somewhere was told something he didn’t want to hear.

“I’m not asking you to forgive me,” said Song Weiren. “I’m too old to be forgiven over a lunch. I just didn’t want you to think nobody in that house saw.”

“Thank you for telling me,” said Aurelia, and found that her voice was not quite steady, and that she didn’t mind him hearing it.

When Chen Si came back in he looked once at her face and once at her father’s, and sat down, and said nothing, and moved his water glass so that it stood beside hers.

Over coffee he asked about the collar, and her face changed as she told him: the hundred and four rejected stones, the curve, the trouble of making a thing that heavy look like it weighed nothing.

“You love it.”

“I do. The first collection proved I could do it. This proves I know what I’m doing.”

“That’s quite a difference.” He turned his cup on its saucer. “You’ve become very brave, Aurelia. Braver than I was at your age. Braver than I’ve been for a long time. I should have said so before.”

The old instinct rose in her at once: to smile, to make it easy for him, to tell him it was all right. It wasn’t. Not yet.

“Yes,” she said. “Thank you, Ba.”

It was what she had to give him, and for now it would do.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she looked out of the window and he let her, for a minute, and then took her hand.

“How do you feel?”

“Complicated. Did you believe him?”

“That he didn’t know the whole of it? Yes. And he told us about the fifteen per cent because he wanted us to understand why he was asking. I don’t think he came to lunch meaning to deceive us.”

“You’re being generous.”

“I’m being careful.”

She put her head back on the seat. “Fu Kang. Fifteen per cent for doing nothing. And Fu wants a letter from you.”

“Yes.”

“Then we don’t give him one.” She turned her head. “Can you make Fu sign the approvals?”

“Eventually.”

“How?”

“Not with a letter. You won’t like the rest.”

“Try me.”

“Fu has spent twenty years making sure nobody can ever put him in a position where he has to sign anything.”

“Then we change the position,” said Aurelia. “He asked for fifteen per cent for his son. If his son’s part of the arrangement, then his son’s the soft place in it. I want Fu to understand his boy isn’t an untouchable bargaining chip.”

“Aurelia.”

“I’m not suggesting anyone hurts him.”

“I know.”

“Then stop looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re already planning to lock me in the flat.”

“That would be a poor strategy.”

“Very poor.”

He kissed the inside of her wrist, and then didn’t let go, and drew her across the seat until she was tucked against his chest.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping you close.”

“I was already close.”

“Not close enough.” He brushed her cheek with his thumb. “You don’t have to involve yourself in Fu. Your father’s business isn’t yours to carry.”

“Fu involved himself in us. He wants you to go to him. He thinks he can use my father to get to you.” She touched his jaw. “And I’m tired of men deciding that everyone around them is a piece on a board. I don’t want you doing this alone.”

He kissed her. Not the way she’d kissed him against the door on Saturday night. Slower. His hand at the back of her head, as if there were nothing in the world he had to be anywhere for.

“You’re very stubborn,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Very clever. Occasionally reckless.”

“You’re making me sound wonderful.”

“You are.” He held her hand between both of his. He didn’t say yes. He didn’t say no. “Tell me what you have in mind.”

“Not in the car.”

“Why?”

“Qian is driving.”

In the front seat Qian kept his eyes very firmly on the road.

“He’s heard worse,” said Chen Si.

“That isn’t reassuring,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she found him in the study with the Fu report open and the list of nineteen beside it, with the last name where it always was. She put a cup of tea by his hand.

She told him what her father had said while he was out on the pavement, about the fool, and the train, and the cigar. He listened without interrupting once. When she’d finished he said only, “He saw,” and she said, “Yes,” and that was all either of them needed to say about it.

“Is Fu Kang on your list?”

“No. He had nothing to do with what happened to my father. He was eleven.”

“But he’s the reason Fu wants fifteen per cent.”

“That doesn’t make him answerable for his father.”

She knew he was right. She also knew the son might be the one place where the father could be made to bend.

“Then we find out what he wants. Carefully.”

“And we don’t assume he’s like his father.”

“Agreed.” She leaned on the desk. “You won’t move without telling me.”

“Is that an order?”

“No. A request.”

“Then I’ll make you the same one.”

“Agreed.”

She picked up the black jade queen from beside the report and turned it in her fingers. “Fu’s spent twenty years believing nobody can make him answer for anything.”

“Yes.”

She put the queen down on the paper, over his name, where she’d put it in August.

“Let’s see how he feels,” said Aurelia, “when somebody finally makes him sign.”

His mouth curved, and his eyes stayed serious, and he reached for her hand.

“Together,” he said.

“Together,” said Aurelia.

chapters.title: Aurelia Says No to Her Mother
chapters.desc: She tells her mother no in front of the maids. Then she and Mr. Lu work out how to get at Fu through his son.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you don’t know him.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past eight on the Friday, Chen Si sent his wife a message.

Mr. Thursday: Win.

She was at her dressing table with one earring in and the other between her fingers.

Aurelia: That’s your whole contribution?

Mr. Thursday: I could send flowers.

Aurelia: Too late. I’m dressed.

Mr. Thursday: Then I’ll send a better husband.

Aurelia: I don’t want another one.

Mr. Thursday: Good. He’s difficult to replace.

She put the second earring in and looked at herself. Ivory blouse, black trousers, a narrow gold belt, the small diamond studs he’d given her the night the second shop opened. Hair pinned low. Nothing extravagant. Nothing anybody could mistake for armour. She didn’t need armour to talk to her mother. That was what she intended to believe.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria was in the morning room at the house on the Peak, by the tall windows with her tea and a stack of letters. Three maids were in the room: one doing the lilies, one laying the breakfast tray, one gathering yesterday’s papers.

“Mother.”

“You’re up early. Sit down.”

“I’ll stand.”

Vittoria’s eyes went over her clothes and paused on the earrings. “Those are pretty. Your husband?”

Aurelia didn’t answer that.

“Did you see your father after lunch?”

“He told me about Fu’s offer. Fifteen per cent for Fu Kang. And he told me what you called him when he refused.”

Vittoria’s hand stopped over the letter. “That was a private conversation.”

“Then you shouldn’t have had it in front of the staff.”

The maid with the lilies lowered her eyes.

“Business isn’t always as simple as you’d like, Aurelia.”

“Fifteen per cent in exchange for approvals is very simple.”

“Fu has considerable influence.”

“Then he can use it to earn his own money.”

“You’re being childish.”

“I’m being specific. Did you call Ba a fool because he said no to Fu?”

Vittoria’s mouth thinned. “I called him a fool because he wouldn’t consider the consequences.”

“So you did.”

“He has a duty to the company.”

“He has a duty not to hand a sixth of it to someone else’s son for nothing.”

“Fu Kang would have brought connections.”

“Then he could have negotiated for what he’s actually worth.” Aurelia didn’t raise her voice. “And you could have stopped short of asking my husband to write to a man with his father’s blood on his hands.”

The room went very still. The maid with the tray stopped moving.

“Lower your voice,” said Vittoria. “There are people here.”

“Yes. I can see that.”

“Don’t make a spectacle.”

“I’m not the one who carried a business arrangement into my marriage.”

“You think marriage makes you untouchable?”

“I think it gives me the right to decide what I will and won’t ask my husband to do. He told you no. That was his reason. No.”

Vittoria put her cup down. “You’ve become very difficult since you married him.”

“How interesting. I thought I’d always been difficult.”

“You used to know when to listen.”

“I used to know when to keep quiet,” said Aurelia.

Vittoria stood up. “Aurelia—“

“No.”

It came out quietly. Vittoria blinked. Aurelia said it again, in the language of the city she’d been born in, the one her grandfather had taught her mahjong in, clearly and slowly.

“No. You won’t ask Chen Si to go to Fu again. You won’t ask Ba to persuade him. And you won’t use my marriage to get anything out of anyone.”

“You can’t dictate what I say to your father.”

“Then say it to him. Leave my husband out of it. If you don’t, I’ll cut every thread between my house and yours. No introductions. No shared clients. No use of my name or my designs or my people for anything of yours. You won’t walk into my shops and speak to my staff as if you own them. And if you try it again after that, it’s permanent.”

“You’d do that? To your own mother?”

There it was. The question that had sent her backing out of rooms her whole life. Would you really do that to your own mother? Would you really make her unhappy? Would you really choose yourself?

Aurelia took a breath. “I hope I never have to.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I’m giving you.”

“You’ve become arrogant.”

“No. Clear.”

She was at the door when her mother spoke again.

“You think he’ll always put you first? Men like that don’t respect women. They indulge them, until they become inconvenient.”

Aurelia stopped. She thought of him on his knees on his own rug. Of his wrists in black silk on a workbench, waiting. Of the hall of their flat, his phone in his hand, turning off a thing he should never have turned on, because she’d asked. He wasn’t an easy man. He wasn’t a harmless one. But he’d never once asked her to mistake obedience for love.

When she turned round, her face was almost gentle.

“Then you don’t know him,” she said, and went.

Behind her, the maid by the window went back to the lilies.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she sat with her hands folded in her lap and waited to feel triumphant. She felt hollow. It had taken ten minutes. It had taken her twenty-four years to be able to do it.

Mr. Thursday: How did it go?

Aurelia: I said no.

Mr. Thursday: I know.

Aurelia: How?

Mr. Thursday: You haven’t rung me to complain. So you’re either satisfied or furious.

Aurelia: I can be both.

Mr. Thursday: I know that too.

Aurelia: You only have one word for me this morning?

Mr. Thursday: I have several. I’m saving them until I see you.

A minute later:

Mr. Thursday: I’m proud of you.

She held the phone in both hands and looked out at the harbour going by, and the tight thing in her chest eased by a small degree.

✦ ✦ ✦

At that hour Chen Si was in the harbour office with the Morning Star lying at the quay outside the window, due to sail at four, and Mr. Tam standing in front of the desk looking as though he’d have given a year of his life to be elsewhere.

“Your cousin,” said Chen Si, without looking up.

“He says it was a misunderstanding. He’s agreed to pay it back. Most of it.”

“Most.”

“He’s trying to find the rest.”

“Then he can find it somewhere else.” Chen Si closed the folder. “He was given a shipping account. He used it to divert payments and fake invoices, and he let three clerks answer for money they’d never touched. One of them was questioned by the police.”

“I didn’t know.”

“That may be true. It doesn’t make the damage go away.”

Qian opened his own folder. “His position’s ended. His debts are being recovered through the courts. He’s posted to inventory at the southern yard. The Morning Star sails at four.”

Mr. Tam went grey. “The south? He’s never lived outside the city. The conditions down there—“

“Aren’t fatal.” Chen Si’s voice was mild, which made it worse. “He’ll have a bed, a wage, and a job that makes him count every box he touches. If he steals again, the next conversation won’t be about his employment. You recommended him. You’ll see he doesn’t come back to this office without my say.”

When the door had closed, Qian said, “Someone to go with him?”

“One supervisor. No special treatment. Is Mr. Yuen here?”

“In the conference room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Yuen was in his late fifties, silver at the temples, with a way of looking round a room before he decided where to sit. He’d been Chen Rong’s lawyer once, before the arrest, and had come back to the son ten years later without being asked. He knew where respectable money and the other kind tended to meet, and how they shook hands.

Aurelia came in twenty minutes after him with a slim leather notebook. Chen Si stood and pulled out the chair beside his own and put a glass of water in front of her.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

She gave him a look. Mr. Yuen studied his notes with great interest.

“Fu Kang has expensive tastes,” he said, and slid a photograph across the table: a wristwatch, old, very rare, with a movement so complicated that only a handful had ever been made. “Seven like this in eighteen months. From private dealers and through people who bid for others at auction. Never in his own name. They’re bought by an offshore company that deals in collectables on paper and has never sold anything to anyone. The directors on the register aren’t the owners. We have reason to believe it acts for Fu Kang.”

“Reason to believe,” said Aurelia.

“Patterns. Repeated contacts. Payments that line up. Not enough to write his name on an accusation.”

“Then we don’t.”

“Precisely,” said Mr. Yuen, and looked at her with something like respect. “Some of the watches sit in private collections. Some are sold on. Some he’s borrowed against.”

“He’s buying things that hold their value, are easy to carry, and don’t need explaining,” said Aurelia.

“That’s one way to put it.”

“Is the company tied to Fu’s business?”

“Not directly. But one of the go-betweens once worked for a firm in Fu’s development interests.” He named the man. Qian wrote it down.

“Fu Kang wants fifteen per cent of a bridge,” said Aurelia slowly, “and already has a drawer full of watches. So he doesn’t need the bridge for the money.”

“What do you think he wants?” said Chen Si.

“Legitimacy. Something his father can point at and call a respectable investment.” She tapped the photograph. “And if he buys like this he knows the dealers, the collectors, the auction rooms, the people who handle private sales. That’s my world. Not yours.”

“You want to come at him through the watches.”

“I want to understand why he buys them. That’s not the same thing.”

“There’s another possibility,” said Mr. Yuen. “Four of the pieces were bought within weeks of Fu first making demands on the bridge. Three through the same company. The fourth through a dealer overseas.”

Chen Si’s finger tapped the table once. “Fu may be using his son’s collection to move value outside his own books.”

“Possibly. I wouldn’t draw that conclusion yet.”

“We need the records, not guesses,” said Aurelia.

“Exactly,” said Mr. Yuen, pleased.

Chen Si watched her writing. He knew the look. It was what happened to her face when a problem stopped being an insult and became something she could work on.

“Can you find the dealers?” she said.

“Some. The private go-betweens will take longer.”

“Start with the ones we can prove.”

“And what will you do with them?”

“Find out whether Fu Kang is a collector, a businessman, or just his father’s convenient front,” said Aurelia. “They’re very different things.”

“Expensive differences,” said Mr. Yuen.

“Very.”

When he’d gone she sat on, looking at the watch.

“Why watches?” she said. “Not cars, not paintings. A watch is personal. Men buy them because they want to own something rare, because they want to be connected to the person who made it. And it’s one of the few beautiful things a man can collect without ever having to explain himself.”

“You’re describing your clients.”

“I’m describing a market. If he’s using them to move money, he needs people who trust him enough to handle them. He’s building relationships, not just hiding things.” She turned in the chair. “Fu expects you to go to him. Fu Kang might not expect me.”

He looked at her for a moment and bent and kissed her forehead. “Carefully.”

“Always.”

He gave her a look.

“Usually,” she amended.

“Better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home later than she’d meant to and found him in their bedroom beside the dressing table with her jewellery box open.

“What are you doing?”

“Waiting for you. May I?”

“You’re asking to take my earrings out?”

“I’ve learned you’re particular about your things.”

“Very.”

He took out the first earring, and the second, and laid each in its place. She lifted her hair and he unclasped the necklace and let the chain run slowly off her skin, and his fingers stayed a moment at the back of her neck, without any weight in them at all. Then the bracelet. Then the rings.

“You’re stripping me of my assets.”

“Only the portable ones. Did the cousin go?”

“The Morning Star sailed at four.”

“Will he survive?”

“He has a job, a bed and a wage. He’s also been told not to steal.”

He turned her round by the waist. “How are you?”

Not how had the meeting gone. Not had she eaten. How are you.

“I think I did the right thing. I don’t feel very good about it. She made me feel as if I were abandoning her.”

“Were you?”

“No.”

“Then don’t accept the charge.”

“You’re annoyingly sensible.”

“So my wife tells me.”

“She sounds intelligent.”

“Very,” said Chen Si, and kissed her, once, and then again for longer. “Do you want to talk about something else?”

“No.”

“Then what do you want?”

“You. Without having to explain the day first.”

“That I can do.”

He opened the drawer of the bedside cabinet and took out the black silk cuffs she’d left there in the summer, and held them up.

“Do you want them?”

She looked at him for a moment. Then she held out her hands.

He fastened the first round her wrist and checked it with two fingers, and the second, and drew her hands up over her head and tied the silk to the padded headboard, secure without pulling at her shoulders, and stood back to look.

“Admiring your work?”

“Checking it. Comfortable? Hands? Shoulders?”

“Fine. The word’s Milan. Kiss me.”

He did, slowly, giving her time to meet him and to turn her head and to draw him in as far as the silk would let her, and she made a small impatient sound and felt him smile against her mouth.

“You’re taking too long.”

“You asked me to kiss you. I’m doing exactly that.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much,” he said, and kissed the corner of her mouth, and her cheek, and the place under her ear, and her mother’s voice and Fu Kang’s watches and the ship going south all went somewhere a long way off. There was the low lamp and the silk at her wrists and his whole attention, and nothing else, for a long time.

When at last he untied her he rubbed the faint marks on her wrists with his thumbs and waited while she stretched.

“All right?”

She caught his hand and kissed it. “Very.” And then she reached for him, and he came, and the rest of the night was theirs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, with her cheek on his chest, she said, “Will she ring tomorrow?”

“Probably.”

“Will she apologise?”

“No.”

“You’re supposed to comfort me.”

“I could lie.”

“Don’t.”

“She may understand one day. I wouldn’t hang your peace on it.”

“Sometimes I still want her to be proud of me. Even now.”

“I know.”

He didn’t tell her she shouldn’t want it. He held her.

“I want to see the watch records,” she said after a while. “I might be able to reach one of the dealers through the auction houses.”

“You might.”

“You’re not going to tell me to stay out of it?”

“You’ve already decided. Arguing with you before breakfast is a poor investment.” He drew the blanket up. “But Fu Kang isn’t his father. We find out who he is before we decide what he deserves. And if you meet him, I want to know where you are.”

“Location sharing. Both ways. No Qian looking into my appointments. No arranging my life because you think you know better.”

“Agreed.”

“You’re very cooperative tonight.”

“I’m hoping you’ll go on liking me.”

“Unfortunately, I do,” said Aurelia, and kissed his chin, and closed her eyes. For once she hadn’t spent the day trying to be understood. She’d decided what she would allow. It seemed a reasonable place to begin.

chapters.title: Her Mother’s Last Card
chapters.desc: Her mother sends a photograph of Serafina at a street race and names her price. Aurelia keeps it from Chen Si for one night and goes to the garage under the railway bridge.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not angry that you were frightened.”
chapters.content:
The photograph came at seventeen minutes past nine on the last Wednesday in October, while Aurelia was at the bench checking the last claw on a pair of sapphire earrings. Her mother’s name lit up beside the loupe.

A girl in a black racing jacket beside a silver car, under the hard white lights of an underground car park. Hair tied back, face half turned away, one hand on the roof of the car and the other holding a helmet. Graffiti on a concrete pillar behind her. A strip of red tape across the floor. A crowd behind the cars.

Serafina.

Vittoria: Your sister has become rather careless about her company.

Vittoria: I thought you should know where she spends her evenings.

Aurelia’s fingers went cold. A third message came, and a fourth.

Vittoria: I have the registration numbers of several of those cars. The police would be very interested.

Vittoria: I want your husband to write to Fu Jianguo. A proper letter. No more of this ridiculous refusal. You will come to dinner with me on Friday, and smile, and behave as my daughter, and make sure Chen Si gives Fu what he wants.

Vittoria: Or Serafina can explain herself to the police.

For a moment the workshop disappeared. The bench, the lamps, the half-finished earrings, the clock on the wall. There was only her sister beside that car.

She rang Serafina. Nothing. She rang again. Nothing. She rang her mother, who answered on the second ring.

“Good evening, Aurelia.”

“Where did you get that photograph?”

“Does it matter?”

“Who took it?”

“Someone concerned enough to send it to me.”

“If anything happens to Serafina—“

“Then you should tell your husband to write the letter.”

“You’re threatening your own daughter.”

“I’m giving you a choice.”

“No. You’re making a threat and calling it a choice.”

“Don’t be dramatic. I’m protecting this family.”

“By threatening Serafina?”

“By asking you for something very simple. If you refuse, I’ll stop protecting her from the consequences of what she does.”

“She’s your daughter.”

“Then she should behave like it,” said Vittoria, and rang off.

Aurelia stood with the dead phone against her ear. She’d always known her mother could be cruel. She hadn’t known she could be this precise. Vittoria hadn’t aimed at Chen Si. She’d aimed at the one person Aurelia couldn’t bear to see hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

Enzo heard her from the workroom and found her on her knees by the basin in the little washroom, sick, one hand on the porcelain and the other arm wrapped round her stomach. He didn’t say anything. He gathered her hair back off her face and held it, with his other hand flat between her shoulders, until it was over.

“Breathe,” he said. “Easy.”

When she sat back against the wall he gave her a clean cloth and crouched in front of her.

“Darling, I’ve worked with you long enough to know that nothing doesn’t make you look like this.”

She showed him the phone.

“She wants Chen Si to write to Fu,” Aurelia said. “And she’s using Serafina to make him.”

Enzo’s face hardened. “You’re not responsible for your mother’s cruelty.”

“I know.”

“Do you? You’re allowed to be frightened. You don’t have to make it into a business problem.”

Her eyes burned. She hated crying in the workshop. She hated the weakness in her knees. She hated that her mother had found the precise place that made her sixteen.

“I don’t know what to do.”

“Then we start with the girl in the photograph. Not with your mother.”

Her phone buzzed on the tiles.

Mr. Thursday: Leaving the office. Shall I bring dinner?

She looked at it. She could see exactly what would happen if she told him. The stillness coming over his face. Qian on the telephone. Cars going out. Men at that car park before she’d even decided what she wanted. And her mother finding out he knew, and doing God knew what next.

Aurelia: Don’t wait for me. I’ll be late.

Mr. Thursday: Are you all right?

Her thumb hung over the screen.

Aurelia: Just tired.

She put the phone face down. Enzo looked at her.

“You’re not going to tell him?”

“Not tonight,” said Aurelia, to Enzo and to the phone and to herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter to eleven Chen Si knew something was wrong. He sat in the study with a report open in front of him and read the same paragraph four times.

At six minutes past eleven he opened the app they’d both agreed to. Her dot was at the workshop. At eleven forty-two it moved, along the river, to a café near the old circuit where Serafina used to sit as a teenager, and stayed there eleven minutes. Then to a garage under the eastern flyover. Then to another.

He didn’t ring Qian. He didn’t send anyone. They’d made an agreement in the hall of this flat: no tracking in secret, no devices, no men looking into her appointments. He could see where she was because she’d chosen to let him. That didn’t mean he was entitled to know what she was doing there.

Chen Si: Are you coming home?

No answer.

Chen Si: I can come and get you.

No answer. At fourteen minutes past one he rang, and it rang out.

He put the phone down. He picked it up again. He could have sent Qian to the café. He could have rung Enzo and demanded an explanation. He did none of those things. He sat in the study for five hours and watched a small blue dot cross the city, from garage to garage to her shop, and at six minutes past four it came home.

He was still awake when she opened the bedroom door.

“You’re awake.”

“You weren’t home.”

“I told you I’d be late.”

“You did.”

He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t ask where she’d been. That was worse. She came and kissed his cheek and said she was sorry, and he caught her hand.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

He searched her face. She held his eyes. For a moment it looked as though he’d ask something else. Then he let go.

“Go to bed.”

When the bathroom door had closed, he looked once more at the screen, and turned the screen off. Not the sharing. The screen.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a note by her coffee in his engraved hand. Eat something before you start work. No message from Vittoria. And then, at last, her sister’s voice, thick with sleep.

“Aurelia?”

“Where are you?”

“At home. Why?”

“Where were you last night?”

“With friends.”

“At a race?”

Silence. “Who told you? Did Mother ring you?” A short laugh. “Of course she did.”

“Are you racing tonight?”

“No.”

“Promise me.”

“Aurelia—“

“Please.”

It came out smaller than she’d meant. Serafina was quiet.

“I’m not racing tonight.”

“I’ll ring you later.”

She sat with the phone in her lap for a long time afterwards. One more night. One night to find a way out before she told him. She knew it was a bad plan. She knew she was going to do it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight on the Thursday she got out of her car under the railway bridge, where the tracks threw long shadows across a row of dead warehouses and a train went over every eleven minutes, shaking dust down off the beams. Modified cars everywhere, bonnets up. Groups of people smoking and shouting over the engines. She’d worn a dark coat and low heels, and left all her jewellery at home.

“Looking for someone?” said a man at the entrance.

“Tell Serafina her sister’s here.”

Serafina came out a minute later in the black jacket from the photograph, and her face changed.

“What are you doing here?”

“That’s a lovely greeting.”

“You’re not supposed to be here.”

“Neither are you, apparently. Mother has a photograph. And registration numbers.”

They walked round the side of the building away from the noise. Serafina folded her arms. She looked older than the girl with the plastic necklace. Sharper round the eyes. When she frowned she still had the same small crease between her brows.

“I like it here,” she said, before Aurelia could ask.

“You could be arrested.”

“I’m not stupid.”

“That isn’t what I said. I don’t want a telephone call at three in the morning telling me you’re in a police station.”

“You’re not my mother.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t talk to me like her.”

Aurelia flinched. Serafina saw it, and her face softened, and she didn’t apologise.

“I didn’t come to tell you what to do,” said Aurelia. “I came because I was worried. And because I want you to stop putting yourself where she can use you.”

Serafina went still. “Use me for what?”

Aurelia didn’t answer fast enough.

“Oh my God. She’s blackmailing you.”

“Serafina—“

“What does she want?”

“A letter. From Chen Si. To Fu Jianguo.”

Serafina stared at her. “After everything? She’s using me to make your husband crawl to Fu?” She swore, short and filthy, the way she’d learned in pit lanes. “That bitch.”

“Don’t.”

“You’re not going to do it.”

“No. But I need you to stop giving her material.”

“I don’t need you running my life.”

“I know.” Aurelia looked at the cars, the crowd, the dark under the bridge. “I don’t want to run it. I want you to be able to choose what happens to you without her holding it over your head.”

Serafina looked at her for a long time. Then she said, very quietly, “She doesn’t know everything. She knows about the races. She doesn’t know about the rest.” A beat. “You really don’t know?”

“Know what?”

“You’re the sponsor.” Serafina took out her phone and opened a folder and held it out. Transfer receipts. Three years of them, quarterly, to a small racing team in the north of the city. The sender a company with a dull name. “Don’t pretend.”

Aurelia looked at the reference numbers, and knew them. She’d authorised them herself. Three years ago a small team with no money had written asking for help with safety equipment, and she’d seen whose name was on the driver list, and quietly arranged it through a subsidiary, and told the team never to say where it came from. She’d never told Serafina. She’d assumed nobody would.

“You found out,” she said.

“Last year. One of the mechanics got drunk.” Serafina’s voice wobbled. “I thought you were doing it so you wouldn’t have to talk to me. Paying me to go away.”

“No.”

“Then why?”

Because you were the only one of us who ever looked happy talking about something you loved. Because I remembered you crying when they took away your first helmet. Because you were always brave enough to want things without asking whether it would make her proud. Because I couldn’t give you the freedom I never had, but I could at least help pay for it.

“Because you loved racing,” she said.

“That’s it?”

“Isn’t that enough?”

Serafina looked away. For a moment she seemed about nine years old. Then she laughed, and it wasn’t steady.

“You idiot.”

“That’s very rude to your sponsor.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t want you to think you owed me anything.”

Serafina stepped forward and hugged her, sudden and awkward and fierce. “I thought you didn’t care,” she said into Aurelia’s coat.

“Never,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat for an hour on the bonnet of a dead car outside the garage while the trains went over. Serafina told her about the team, and the mechanics, and why she came here. Not because it was where she wanted to end up. Because it was where she came when she couldn’t find any other way to feel alive. Somewhere she could be good at a thing without being measured against their mother, or their father, or her sister.

“There’s a race on the twenty-first of December,” she said at last. “A proper one. Closed circuit, permits, safety crews. I’m entered.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Because nobody here asks me to be respectable.”

“Would you rather race somewhere you could build something?”

“What does that mean?”

“It means we do the twenty-first properly. A real sponsorship. Your team, your car, your name, and mine on the side of it where everybody can see. AURELIA. No more anonymous transfers.”

Serafina stared. “People will say you bought my place.”

“Then we’ll make sure you earn it.”

“Mother will hate it.”

“That isn’t a deciding factor,” said Aurelia, and Serafina laughed out loud.

“And you won’t interfere with my racing?”

“I’ll interfere with the illegal parts. I’ll pay for the team and sort the contracts and make sure it’s safe. You drive your own race.”

Serafina held out her oily hand, and Aurelia shook it, and then because they were sisters and neither of them could bear to be sentimental for long, Serafina dragged her into another hug and left a black smear across her cheek.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was in the sitting room when she came in after midnight. Not reading. His phone face down on the table. That was the first thing she noticed.

“You’re late.”

“I was with Serafina.”

His face changed. “Is she all right?”

“Yes.”

He stood and came to her and saw the smear of oil on her cheek. He took a soft cloth from the side table and wiped it away, very gently.

“You’re not going to tell me where you’ve been?”

“I need to tell you something. Can we sit?”

They sat. She folded her hands in her lap, and told him. The photograph. The registration numbers. Friday dinner, and the smile, and the letter to Fu.

He didn’t interrupt. His face didn’t change. But his hand closed slowly round hers until she could feel the bones of his fingers.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I was frightened. Of what you’d do. You’d have sent Qian. You’d have found everyone who took that photograph and everyone who’d ever stood in that car park, and you might have gone after my mother before I knew what I wanted. I didn’t want to decide anything while I was that frightened.”

“So you went to a garage under a railway bridge. Alone.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t look at me like that,” she said.

“I’m thinking several things.”

“Such as?”

“That your mother is more dangerous than I’d allowed for. That you went somewhere unsafe without telling me. That I spent five hours in that chair watching a dot cross the city and trying not to break an agreement we’d made in our own hall.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Is Serafina safe?”

“Yes.” And she told him the rest: the transfers, three years of them, and her sister calling her an idiot.

His mouth moved. “Reasonable.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. I can agree with her as well.” He drew her in, and she leaned against him, and her eyes filled without warning. “She thought I didn’t care.”

“She knows now.”

“The twenty-first of December. A proper race. Our sponsorship, in daylight.”

“Then we’ll read the contracts before anyone signs anything.”

“Of course you’d say that.”

“I’d be a poor husband if I let you sign a sponsorship without reading the terms.”

“You’re a very annoying husband.”

“And yet you keep him,” said Chen Si. Then his face went quiet. “Your mother has registration numbers. By tomorrow night she won’t have the man who took the photograph. Nobody will hurt him. He’ll find he’s been offered a very good job a long way away, and that he’d like to take it.” He looked at her. “That’s what I want to do. I’m asking you.”

She looked back at him for a long moment. “Ask me again in the morning. If I still say yes, do it.”

“All right.” He turned her hand over in his. “She used Serafina because she knew you’d come. She was counting on you being too frightened to tell me.”

“She was right.”

He didn’t look pleased. He didn’t punish her for it either. “Next time, tell me before you go.”

“Next time I will.”

“And I won’t decide anything for you without asking. Especially when I think it’s necessary.”

She put her hand to his face, and he turned his head and kissed her palm.

“Thank you for waiting,” she whispered.

He kissed her then, slowly at first, his hand at her jaw, and then she moved closer and he pulled her into his arms and kissed her as if he’d been holding a question in his mouth for five hours and had decided, finally, not to ask it.

“I’m not angry that you were frightened,” he said against her hair. “I’m angry that she made you think you had to carry it on your own. That isn’t the same thing.”

He held her for a while. Then he looked at the clock.

“Have you eaten?”

She stared at him. “I’ve just told you my mother blackmailed me with my sister.”

“I heard. Have you eaten?”

She laughed, properly, for the first time since the photograph. “No.”

“Stay there,” said Chen Si, and went into the kitchen, and she heard him get out the rice.

Her phone buzzed.

Serafina: Don’t tell Mother about December yet.

Aurelia: I won’t.

Serafina: And thank you.

Aurelia: You don’t owe me anything. Just drive safely.

She put the phone down. Her mother had wanted a letter, and a smile, and a daughter who came when she was called. Instead she’d handed Aurelia a reason to stop keeping her sister a secret. On the twenty-first of December Serafina would race under her own name, and down the side of her car, in letters a foot high, would be Aurelia’s.

chapters.title: The Racing Team She Pretends Not to Fund
chapters.desc: Aurelia sells Fu Kang a watch from Geneva and follows his money all the way to his father’s name. She also learns to change a wheel and rebuilds her sister’s sponsorship deck in one night.
chapters.epigraph: “Then he’ll have to learn I’m not very easy to persuade.”
chapters.content:
Monsieur Aubert had not sold a watch to a man he disliked in thirty years. He’d made the rule after a collector tried to pay him with money that smelled of a minister’s missing millions. He’d made a second rule soon after: he didn’t sell to men who thought money made them interesting.

“Fu Kang, unfortunately,” he said, “appears to be both.”
